speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: REFERENCE TO STATEMENT BY DEPUTY POSTMASTER GENERAL RESPECTING ROBBERIES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask a question of the Acting Postmaster General. Did the Acting Postmaster General authorize a statement made yesterday in the press by the deputy postmaster general with respect to charges I made in this house on June 20 concerning post office thefts?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. W. Pickersgill (Acting Postmaster General):
speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
subtopic: REFERENCE TO STATEMENT BY DEPUTY POSTMASTER GENERAL RESPECTING ROBBERIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I spoke to the deputy postmaster general about an item which appeared in one newspaper yesterday, and I have not seen it in any other. There was no interview given by the deputy postmaster general to any pressman yesterday.
I am told that on the day before yesterday when I was absent from Ottawa and the parliamentary assistant to the postmaster general was also absent, the deputy postmaster general was approached by a journalist in the press gallery with a copy of a return which was made some time ago in this house about postal robberies, and that a number of questions were put to him; and he gave some answers to those questions, of which a report appears on page 7 of yesterday's Evening Citizen.

Inquiries of the Ministry
I told the deputy postmaster general that, in view of the fact that the hon. member for Quebec West had raised certain questions in the house, I rather regretted that any statement had appeared or been made to any journalist about this matter before there was an opportunity for the responsible minister to speak about it in the house. I think the deputy postmaster general also regrets that.

subtopic: REFERENCE TO STATEMENT BY DEPUTY POSTMASTER GENERAL RESPECTING ROBBERIES
speechtext: You cannot be sure of that.

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
subtopic: REFERENCE TO STATEMENT BY DEPUTY POSTMASTER GENERAL RESPECTING ROBBERIES
speechtext: I can however be sure of one thing. I was a civil servant for a great many years, and I know how difficult it is when false and misleading charges are made about civil servants to remain silent on every occasion-though, in fact, during the whole time that I was a public servant I never gave any statement to the press on any occasion, and I never answered any question unless I was authorized to do so by the minister to whom I was responsible.

speakeroldname: Hon. George A. Drew (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: REFERENCE TO STATEMENT BY DEPUTY POSTMASTER GENERAL RESPECTING ROBBERIES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think the minister is in duty bound, in view of the nature of the subject matter, to make it perfectly clear to whom he is referring and to what remarks he is referring when he speaks about false and misleading statements.

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
subtopic: REFERENCE TO STATEMENT BY DEPUTY POSTMASTER GENERAL RESPECTING ROBBERIES
speechtext: I am referring to a great number of false and misleading statements that have been made in and outside the house on a great many occasions about a great many civil servants, and I have nothing particular or specific in mind.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: REFERENCE TO STATEMENT BY DEPUTY POSTMASTER GENERAL RESPECTING ROBBERIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is no occasion to press this unduly, beyond the fact that the minister is dealing with a statement in a highly responsible newspaper which gave the impression that the deputy minister had made statements in reference to statements made in this house. Whether the minister agrees or disagrees with the statements that were made, they were made on the responsibility of a member of this house. If the statements of the deputy postmaster general had in fact challenged a statement made in this house it would have been a most improper course.
The minister has now talked about the provocation of false and misleading statements, and I think that he should make it perfectly clear that neither directly nor indirectly is he making any inference in regard to the statement of the hon. member for Quebec West (Mr. Dufresne).

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
subtopic: REFERENCE TO STATEMENT BY DEPUTY POSTMASTER GENERAL RESPECTING ROBBERIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it may be in the knowledge of most hon. members that there is on the notice paper of today a question which is to be answered orally on


Monday, and I intend to answer that question in great detail, and to deal, at that time, with every significant point raised by the hon. member for Quebec West. And I think it would be preferable to have the facts before anything further is said about it.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: REFERENCE TO STATEMENT BY DEPUTY POSTMASTER GENERAL RESPECTING ROBBERIES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I place the matter before you. The remarks that have been made are open to the interpretation that they did refer to a statement made by an hon. member of this house. I submit that it is not good enough to evade that now and to say: "I am placing facts before this house on Monday." The minister who has spoken has the responsibility of removing any uncertainty about the suggestion that the term "false and misleading statements" might have applied to statements made in this house by the hon. member on his responsibility as a member of this house.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: REFERENCE TO STATEMENT BY DEPUTY POSTMASTER GENERAL RESPECTING ROBBERIES
speechtext: The Leader of the Opposition wishes me to consider whether these remarks to the hon. member for Quebec West should be withdrawn?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: REFERENCE TO STATEMENT BY DEPUTY POSTMASTER GENERAL RESPECTING ROBBERIES
speechtext: I submit that unless the minister is prepared to say that neither directly nor indirectly did they apply to the statement made by the hon. member for Quebec West, then he must withdraw them. It is not for the minister to charge any member of this house with making false or misleading statements.

subtopic: REFERENCE TO STATEMENT BY DEPUTY POSTMASTER GENERAL RESPECTING ROBBERIES
speechtext: On the point, I think the minister should be asked to withdraw. He not only referred to the hon. member for Quebec West as an offender, but as I recall it he referred to false and misleading statements made in this house and outside the house. I think that is quite improper language for any minister to use unless he gives specific instances. I, suggest he should be asked to withdraw.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: REFERENCE TO STATEMENT BY DEPUTY POSTMASTER GENERAL RESPECTING ROBBERIES
speechtext:
As one who has been charged on many occasions as being perhaps too severe with expressions used in this house, may I say that I have heard these qualifications attributed to statements on many occasions in the last three weeks, namely that statements are false and misleading. I have heard it said on many occasions. If it is the wish of hon. members to have the expression withdrawn today I see no objection to it myself because there is no specific rule whatever with respect to these things. See citation 234, Beauchesne's third edition. An expression which is deemed to be unparliamentary today does not necessarily have to be deemed unparliamentary next week. We have to consider the various conditions relating to the position which is taken at the time the expressions are used.

If the minister had said directly that the statements made by the hon. member for Quebec West were false and misleading we would have a point in asking that the expression be withdrawn; but he made the statement in a general way. Are we going to prohibit a member from saying that either inside or outside the house with respect to a certain matter there might be false and misleading statements made, without any direct attribution to a member of this house? I do not think so.

subtopic: REFERENCE TO STATEMENT BY DEPUTY POSTMASTER GENERAL RESPECTING ROBBERIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I say this is a point which should not be disposed of without due consideration. As Your Honour has pointed out on a number of occasions in the past, matters of this kind should be dealt with immediately or they are accepted as part of the ordinary exchange in the house. I, for one, do not believe that there should be too great a strain on the application of words and demands for withdrawals. In this particular case the minister did refer to a statement made by the hon. member for Quebec West, and then following that, he referred to the provocation under which civil servants have been as a result of false and misleading statements.
I submit that those words in combination suggest that for the purpose of misleading the house a member has made false and misleading statements. Unless the minister is prepared to say that they did not apply to the hon. member whose statement he had just been discussing, then I think he should be asked to withdraw. Of course, if these are to become an accepted part of the exchange here, then of course there might be a temptation for someone to talk about false and misleading impressions conveyed by ministers of the crown. I do not think that would be a desirable situation. In this case, Your Honour should consider whether these terms are to be accepted as appropriate to statements that have been made on the full responsibility of a member of this house.

subtopic: REFERENCE TO STATEMENT BY DEPUTY POSTMASTER GENERAL RESPECTING ROBBERIES
speechtext: As I recall the words, they were something like "false and misleading, made in and out of this house". I submit that no hon. member and certainly no cabinet minister should be permitted to make that sort of reference without giving specific cases and giving hon. members the opportunity to defend the alleged charges. I submit that the hon. member should be asked to withdraw that statement.

subtopic: REFERENCE TO STATEMENT BY DEPUTY POSTMASTER GENERAL RESPECTING ROBBERIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to say one thing. I had thought that we were becoming too sensitive about things said in this house, but there is one word which does seem to me to be
Inquiries of the Ministry different from any other and that is the allegation of falsehood. Any hon. member can say anything he likes about me except that what I have said is false or anything suggesting untruthfulness.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. E. Harris (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: REFERENCE TO STATEMENT BY DEPUTY POSTMASTER GENERAL RESPECTING ROBBERIES
speechtext: Surely my hon. friend, who has on occasion engaged in discussion of my department, would not expect me to accept as a fact everything he says about it. Then what is wrong if I say that I think it is false?

subtopic: REFERENCE TO STATEMENT BY DEPUTY POSTMASTER GENERAL RESPECTING ROBBERIES
speechtext: Surely there is all the difference in the world between making a mistake-I am admitting to the minister that I make mistakes-and saying something which is false. False implies that you do it with knowledge.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: REFERENCE TO STATEMENT BY DEPUTY POSTMASTER GENERAL RESPECTING ROBBERIES
speechtext:
Let us get on with
the business of the house.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: REFERENCE TO STATEMENT BY DEPUTY POSTMASTER GENERAL RESPECTING ROBBERIES
speechtext: Unless deliberate intention can be attributed to the particular expression which it is asked be withdrawn I do not think I can ask that it be withdrawn. At least two of my colleagues have come to me to discuss the point with me contending that if an hon. member says of another that what he says is a falsehood, the word "falsehood" is not synonymous with untruth, and the word falsehood implies a deliberate untruth. It may be that my knowledge of the English language is not as far advanced as that of some hon. members. I am not going to prolong this discussion and perhaps we can ask the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mr. Pickersgill) to accommodate us and-

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
subtopic: REFERENCE TO STATEMENT BY DEPUTY POSTMASTER GENERAL RESPECTING ROBBERIES
speechtext: I am perfectly happy to-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: REFERENCE TO STATEMENT BY DEPUTY POSTMASTER GENERAL RESPECTING ROBBERIES
speechtext: I am not asking the minister to withdraw, I am simply asking him to accommodate us. Unless I can be shown that the expression was attributed directly to the hon. member for Quebec West (Mr. Dufresne), which I do not think it was, and unless the word "false" implies deliberate intention to say an untruth then I would not ask the minister to withdraw. See citation 257, Beauchesne's third edition.

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
subtopic: REFERENCE TO STATEMENT BY DEPUTY POSTMASTER GENERAL RESPECTING ROBBERIES
speechtext:
I think a statement is either false or it is not false. It is a matter of objective fact. My knowledge of the rules of the house is limited but I attempted to stay within the rules and anything I said implied no motive on the part of anybody. I have made false statements in this house not knowing they were false, and I doubt if there is any hon. member of this house, except some praiseworthy members like the hon. member for Pictou, who does not take up a lot of time unnecessarily, who at times has not, without deliberate intent, said things that turned out to be incorrect, turned out to be false and

Supply-Agriculture
turned out to be misleading. All I did say was that it is sometimes hard to bear things like that in silence, because after all civil servants are human beings. That is all I said and that is all I meant. I was not implying in this particular reference any deliberate intention on the part of anyone.

subtopic: REFERENCE TO STATEMENT BY DEPUTY POSTMASTER GENERAL RESPECTING ROBBERIES
speechtext: The minister has refused to withdraw a reference to a member of this chamber and, Mr. Speaker, I submit that you should examine Hansard when it is available and give a ruling at a later date and state if in your opinion the minister should not be asked to withdraw the reference which he made.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: REFERENCE TO STATEMENT BY DEPUTY POSTMASTER GENERAL RESPECTING ROBBERIES
speechtext: Let us examine this as calmly as we can and review the situation for one moment. The minister has referred to false and misleading charges or statements made in this house or outside of this house.

subtopic: REFERENCE TO STATEMENT BY DEPUTY POSTMASTER GENERAL RESPECTING ROBBERIES
speechtext: By members.

subtopic: REFERENCE TO STATEMENT BY DEPUTY POSTMASTER GENERAL RESPECTING ROBBERIES
speechtext: No.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: REFERENCE TO STATEMENT BY DEPUTY POSTMASTER GENERAL RESPECTING ROBBERIES

speechtext:
I notice that this item is for the sum of something over half a million dollars in the main estimates and that in the supplementaries there is a further sum of about $1J million. Evidently it is a subsidy 50433-420
Supply-Agriculture
arrangement under the Cold Storage Act which is becoming increasingly of value to various agricultural groups. I rise on this item to draw attention to what I consider to be an unnecessary limitation upon the application of the Cold Storage Act as far as eligibility for these subsidies is concerned. It arises out of a situation in my own constituency where a small farmers' co-operative organization applied for a subsidy.
The matter was taken up here and I made some representations on their behalf at the last session. As I understand the situation, the question of their eligibility under the present act was referred to the Department of Justice for determination and the ruling was made that they were not. The particular type of cold storage installation they had in mind is of a prefabricated nature, sometimes known, I believe, as the warm room type of cold storage locker. I think it has developed because of new techniques and production methods and was not contemplated at the time the present act was drawn up. It does appear to me to be a type of installation peculiarly suited to small farmers' organizations who are attempting to get started, sometimes in pioneer areas where they are still in the stage of developing their land.
I think it is unfortunate that such farm organizations should be denied access to the assistance available under the Cold Storage Act as it is now drawn. I therefore hope the parliamentary assistant will give the undertaking that he will draw this matter to the attention of the Minister of Agriculture and ask him to give consideration to the advisability of introducing an amendment to the Cold Storage Act to cover situations of this kind. I believe there are two or three firms in British Columbia producing this type of semi-prefabricated cold storage unit which can be installed in a building already in existence, and that because of the wording of the act this particular type of cold storage installation is not eligible for the subsidies provided under the act.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: REFERENCE TO STATEMENT BY DEPUTY POSTMASTER GENERAL RESPECTING ROBBERIES

We try to be as lenient as we can in the establishing of cold storage plants throughout the length and breadth of Canada because we feel they are very necessary for the preservation and processing of foodstuffs. Of course we have certain rules and regulations that we must follow and we must not depart from them because every effort must be made that can be made to see that such plants are the proper type in which to store food. But we are always glad to look into any case that is

Supply-Agriculture
brought to our attention or any amendment that may be considered necessary.

One could make a long speech on the subject raised by the hon. member, but I think it unnecessary to do so at this time.
As hon. members know, 70 per cent of farm income in Ontario comes from the sale of livestock and livestock products, and of course a great part of farm income in western Canada is also derived from livestock. While they may be grain-growing provinces, livestock represents a large portion of their income.
For the information of hon. members I shall place on record figures showing the difference between marketings in the first six months of 1955 as compared with the first six months of 1954. In the length and breadth of Canada there were marketed 3,158,412 hogs in 1955, up to July 16 of this year. Last year there were marketed 2,614,529 hogs making an increase this year over last year of 20-8 per cent. Also our hog marketing percentages have gone up in western and eastern Canada. In eastern Canada they are up by some 16 per cent and in western Canada by 30-9 per cent over last year.

Then, turning to cattle: Up to July 16 of this year we marketed 992,479 whereas last year we marketed 988,356, or an increase in marketings of -5 per cent. subtopic: REFERENCE TO STATEMENT BY DEPUTY POSTMASTER GENERAL RESPECTING ROBBERIES
speechtext: I have not any intention of objecting to the freight assistance on western feed grains other than to say this. From time to time we get down here screenings on which freight should not be paid at all. I do not know of any way of stopping them from coming down here except by some government order. If the farmers in the west were getting any remuneration out of it, it would not be quite so bad; but as it is, an amount is taken off them as dockage. The screenings are supposed to be recleaned and some of the recleaned screenings are all right. They consist of perhaps one-third wheat particles and they are very good feed. But we get dirt down here that should never be brought down at all and freight should not be paid on it. There should be some conceivable way of stopping that stuff at the head of the lakes. Nobody is getting any advantage out of it unless it is the elevators or somebody else. I do not know who are getting the advantage but they should not get it.

subtopic: REFERENCE TO STATEMENT BY DEPUTY POSTMASTER GENERAL RESPECTING ROBBERIES
speechtext:
I cannot allow this item to pass without saying a word or two on it, although I have spoken on it before this session. We are extremely sorry to see this reduction from $17 million to $15,500,000 on freight assistance on western feed grains, a reduction of $1,500,000. That reduction is a serious matter to farmers-particularly to dairy men and poultry producers-in British Columbia, including those in my constituency. They have registered numerous protests. Farmers organizations and many individuals have written to me about this reduction which comes at a time when their costs are increasing and the prices they are receiving for their goods are going lower. While I am not one who advocates unlimited expenditure-I know we must consider all these expenditures-I must say that I think this is a poor place to start saving money, when it is done at the expense of the farmers of British Columbia, especially at a time when, as I said before, their costs of production are rising and the prices of their commodities are becoming lower.
That is all I have to say at this time except that I should like the parliamentary assistant to inform the house why the government saw fit to reduce the freight assistance on western feed grains at this time when the farmers are not in the position they were in three years ago. Can he give us the reason for this reduction?

I think it should be drawn to the attention of the committee that feed grains from western Canada are brought to the lakehead under the jurisdiction of the wheat board and are rigidly inspected by the board of grain commissioners. The jurisdiction of the board of grain commissioners and the wheat board only extends to the lakehead.
I think the problem arises largely when these feed grains leave the lakehead and pass through the milling plants in the various provinces. These matters are under provincial jurisdiction, and perhaps the provincial governments should take a look at them and see if that is not the cause of some of these complaints.

subtopic: REFERENCE TO STATEMENT BY DEPUTY POSTMASTER GENERAL RESPECTING ROBBERIES
speechtext:
Further to what the hon. member has just said, it is true that the grain crosses the border into Ontario and comes to the lakehead, but Ontario should not be expected to take all the blame. I realize that the Ontario government has to accept responsibility with respect to feed sold in Ontario, but I have said on other occasions that the amount of weed seeds in the grain after leaving the head of the lakes is a disgrace. I am not saying it is the fault of the western provinces, but I do say that once weed seeds have been removed from the grain under the regulations of the board of grain commissioners then no weed seeds should be returned to feed and sold as feed.
I think that is sensible. The western producer does not get paid for it. Everybody knows that these weed seeds are put back into the feed just to bring it within a certain grade. It is a common practice and it is admitted by the elevator companies. That is business, and as long as they can get away with it they will because they are out to make money. But I suggest

Supply-Agriculture
sincerely that once weed seeds have been removed from grain under the regulations of the board of grain commissioners it should be against the law to return weed seeds to feed. I am not saying whether this is a matter that comes under provincial or federal jurisdiction, but I believe the federal and provincial authorities should certainly get together and see that certain amendments are made to the legislation.

subtopic: REFERENCE TO STATEMENT BY DEPUTY POSTMASTER GENERAL RESPECTING ROBBERIES
speechtext:
I should like to endorse what the hon. member has just said. We have had instances in the past winter of No. 1 feed screenings coming into Ontario and being sold to farmers for as high as $57 a ton. These screenings consisted of over 90 per cent wild buckwheat, and that is where I think the mistake is made. When we drew this matter to the attention of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, I understand it was investigated by the board of grain commissioners and there is now a new definition of No. 1 feed screenings requiring that No. 1 feed screenings should contain at least 30 per cent cracked grain. The fact that this is some improvement is all to the good.
I agree with the hon. member who has just spoken when he says that the western producer does not get paid for these screenings. Nevertheless they are being sold at 2J cents per pound, or about $1.50 a bushel. The farmers of the west would be glad to sell their barley, oats and other commodities at that price. If freight assistance is going to be provided then I suggest that the $15 million should be paid on good grain and not on screenings taken out of the farmer's grain when hauled to the elevator. The grain companies take out the screenings at the head of the lakes and are selling a product for which they pay nothing. The product is being foisted upon feeders in Ontario and British Columbia. Instead of giving freight assistance on screenings and wild buckwheat,
I suggest that freight assistance should be given on good feed so that the farmers of eastern Canada will have an opportunity to know the quality of feed that the farmers of the prairies can produce.

The point here is that some $228 million has been paid in freight assistance to move feed grains from western Canada to other parts of Canada.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Prime Minister; Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
subtopic: REFERENCE TO STATEMENT BY DEPUTY POSTMASTER GENERAL RESPECTING ROBBERIES
speechtext:
Certainly it is over a period of years. So far as we are concerned the freight assistance has the advantage of placing western Canada products in eastern markets that much more easily, and from a competitive point of view that is an advantage to us. I am not so sure that the same advantage exists all down the line because the freight assistance means that so far as eastern Canada livestock fed with grain brought to that part of the country with the assistance of a subsidy are concerned there are marketing advantages that are lost to the western producer of livestock. However, that is not the point I rose to speak about at this particular time.
Hon. members are complaining bitterly about weed seeds in feed grain being shipped to eastern Canada. That is regrettable, but if you analyse the whole matter right back to the beginning I think it will be found that it is a question of price. Apparently screenings can be sold at a lower price than clean or regular grains. I stand to be corrected, but I would think that the Ontario government or other governments in this part of the country where feed grain is sold would have the authority to prohibit the sale of dangerous noxious weed seeds within their provinces. We do not look upon wild buckwheat as a particularly serious noxious weed. It is true it is a serious nuisance, but there is a lot of nutritive value in wild buckwheat. The other weed seed that we have difficulty handling in the west is wild oats, but this is also very good feed, particularly when the oats are well matured.
The other part of the screenings is made up largely of cracked grain, cracked wheat, cracked barley and that sort of thing. This is always good feed.
Now, I said a moment ago that I think this thing goes back to the question of price. If the provinces where feed grains are being shipped wish to enact regulations prohibiting the importation of things like pigweed seeds or mustard seeds or some of these other noxious weed seeds, then I think those regulations could be enforced. A lot of people are trying to say that the farmer gets nothing out of the sale of these weed seeds. It is true they are refuse and a darn nuisance and all the rest of it, but if my recollection serves me correctly the farmer is paid for his screenings if his sample of grain carries a percentage of over 3 per cent or 4 per cent. He is paid according to the market price of screenings at this time. In addition to that, in the neighbourhood of one-half of our grain in western Canada is marketed through co-operatives. If there is any profit or gain from the sale of screenings outside the western provinces to eastern feeders, surely that is

reflected back in the balances of these co-operatives at the end of the year. To say that this is a total loss to the farmer, therefore, and that the grain companies get it for nothing, is just not borne out by the facts.
So far as our eastern friends are concerned, I think it comes down solely to a question of price. If you are buying screenings at a lower price than you are able to buy good oats and barley, things of that sort, I say that is the answer to why these things are coming down. Now, the freight assistance is a substantial item. I support the principle of carrying through this vote on the ground that freight rates are a very substantial item in shipping anything from one part of Canada to the other. subtopic: REFERENCE TO STATEMENT BY DEPUTY POSTMASTER GENERAL RESPECTING ROBBERIES
speechtext:
I should like to spend two or three minutes on this item because the question of prairie farm rehabilitation is of great interest to the farmers whom I have the honour to represent. For years there have been repeated requests from farm organizations in British Columbia for the application of the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act to that province. In fact I believe they are asking that it be applied to all provinces in Canada. This desire arises from the fact that they know excellent work has been done under the act in the prairie provinces. I know that there have been various projects carried out in British Columbia under this act, but they have been carried out under estimates without the act being made applicable to the province in general. The farmers of British Columbia consider that that is an inadequate and piecemeal approach and that they should have an opportunity to benefit from the excellent services possible under this act by the inclusion of the province within the terms of the act.
Just to illustrate the opportunities there are for the application of the act to British Columbia I shall take my own constituency. There are 16,000 acres of beautiful black soil in the Lardeau valley which could be drained under the terms of this act and which are now unsettled. There are another 10,000 to 15,000 acres in the Duncan river valley of beautiful black soil which could be drained
Supply-Agriculture
and which have not a settler on them. In addition there are thousands and thousands of acres of producing land where the production could be increased by irrigation or land which is not now settled which could be made ready for settlement by irrigation.
There is a tremendous opportunity in British Columbia for the application of this act, particularly in my district because of the local markets we have in the industrial city of Trail and the commercial city of Nelson for all products except fruits. I have been asked by our farm organizations to again urge the government to consider the extension of this act to the other provinces. We have many young men who want to locate on farms and I think we should do everything possible to provide them with an opportunity to do so. Nature has provided the opportunity in British Columbia in abundance and if this act were made applicable to this province as it is to the prairie provinces it would prove most beneficial to the people of British Columbia and to the people of Canada. I do ask the parliamentary assistant to bring these representations to the attention of the minister and the government, because they have been made repeatedly throughout the years, and our people are looking forward to enjoying the benefits possible under this act, just as the prairie farmer has done ever since this legislation was enacted.

Mr. Chairman, this item is for nearly $4 million and the item which has to do with marshland rehabilitation also calls for a large expenditure. In following the discussion so far on these estimates I have been unable to find one suggestion for a lesser expenditure; usually it is the other way around and hon. members are expressing their opinion that greater amounts should be spent. I was a member of the estimates committee for a short time as we tried to divide up the work among the members from our province. I had expected to find that opposition members would be bitterly critical of expenditures by the departments as they have tried to give the impression that as members of the opposition they are doing a great work in saving the taxpayers of this country millions of dollars.
I have listened to the debate which we have had in this committee waiting for someone, particularly a member of the official opposition, to suggest some way in which money might be saved. Just for a few minutes I should like to express the views of the taxpayers of this country toward the perusal of these estimates that has taken place. On many occasions the official opposition have endeavoured to give the impression that they were carrying the ball in this

chamber in the discussion of estimates. If they are carrying the ball they are certainly making every effort to convince the citizens of this country that they are doing a fine job for the taxpayers. This courageous stand which they are taking in this heat in Ottawa has received quite a bit of publicity in the Tory press, I will admit, but for the first time during this debate-

Hon. members of the opposition have suggested that they are prepared to carry on until the snow flies in order to bring about a great saving for the Canadian taxpayers. We have listened to them for two or three months and I think it is time we put some facts on the record.
One particular item had been reduced from $187,000 to $181,000 and we found the financial critic of the agricultural group in the official opposition getting up and wanting to know why there had been this decrease, why there had not been an increase instead of a decrease. Then there was a discussion in connection with grain subsidies where the item showed a decrease in one of the provinces, and immediately they wanted to know why there should be a decrease. The only instance that I can recall at this time where they were in favour of a decrease was in connection with the refreshments supplied to a certain government boat. Perhaps if some of those who criticized that expenditure had to travel on the waters where that boat goes, in many cases uncharted waters, perhaps if they knew that they would not get back for three, six, twelve months or even two years, they might take a different attitude toward the refreshments supplied.
I have just glanced over these different items but I find that hon. members of the official opposition have suggested greater increases in the amounts provided for the building of bridges, particularly in Montreal and in other sections of Canada. There have been many suggestions for improved facilities in the way of breakwaters all across Canada. When public buildings were being discussed there was hardly a member who did not want a building in his constituency. When airports were being discussed they wanted bigger and wider airports across Canada in 
every province. They were asking that dredging operations be carried on in many provinces of Canada. It was suggested that lifesaving stations should be supplied for the protection of those who operate pleasure boats on the great lakes, although the minister stated that it would cost $12 million or $15 million to get such a service under way, and $4 million to $5 million to maintain it afterward. Enormous irrigation projects have been discussed without any thought of a decrease in the cost.

I will now deal with the item that is under consideration. I often wonder whether the expenditure made in connection with this matter of rehabilitation is money wisely spent. I do not think that I can suggest any reduction because it is a matter of which I have little knowledge. I just want to speak briefly about some circumstances which prevail in the maritime provinces. In some areas, particularly in eastern Canada, we find many vacant farms. I can speak of my own province because I know it very well. There are many vacant farms in my own province. Would it not be better to take the amount which is expended for reclaiming marshlands or other lands and use it in a way which might improve land which we already have and which is ready for occupancy? I firmly believe that it is a matter that should be gone into carefully before large expenditures are made for reclaiming other lands. In my own province I know that you can drive through it from beginning to end and find vacant farms in each and every county in the province. I believe that the money which is voted for this purpose might be more wisely spent if it were spent in an endeavour to have these farms once more put into operation and to get families back on them rather than being spent in reclaiming land that we have practically lost.

I will not put the letter on record but I have letters from dozens of people from Winnipeg Beach, Gimli, Sandy Hook, Matlock and so on right down the lake. subtopic: REFERENCE TO STATEMENT BY DEPUTY POSTMASTER GENERAL RESPECTING ROBBERIES
speechtext: Before we leave this item I wish to refer to the answer the parliamentary assistant gave to the hon. member for Selkirk. subtopic: REFERENCE TO STATEMENT BY DEPUTY POSTMASTER GENERAL RESPECTING ROBBERIES

The Riding mountain, Duck mountain and Porcupine mountain areas are on the extreme western boundary of the province of Manitoba, a very long way from what is known as the interlake area. If it is the intention to share this large sum of $150,000 between both areas, then we will of course be thankful for small mercies, but the information brought down by the parliamentary assistant was that the $150,000 was earmarked for these three watersheds on the extreme western boundary of the province of Manitoba. This item deals with Prairie Farm Assistance Act administration. Can the parliamentary assistant tell us whether any instructions are given by the department in the regulations under the act or by any other means as to the method by which employees shall be secured for the purposes of the act? I have in mind, for example, various districts in my own province and perhaps this applies elsewhere. In the fall when inspections have to be made for the purpose of determining the average yield to qualify for assistance under this act we find very often that inspectors and other employees, particularly inspectors who go out to do the checking, are not farmers. It may be necessary to use the services of someone who is not a farmer. I admit that, but these cases must be very few and far between because
Supply-Agriculture
in nearly every area there should be a sufficient number of farmers capable of going out and doing an inspection job.
In my opinion, they are often more efficient than the one who is not engaged in farming because they are more familiar with the situation. Yet we find in some districts a majority of the inspectors appointed are nonfarmers. They are often business people, professional people from the towns and villages, and they go out and do inspection work among the farmers. This creates a certain amount of resentment-I think justifiably so -particularly in Manitoba, where the farmers have been contributing to the prairie farm assistance fund by way of the 1 per cent deduction approximately three times as much as they have drawn out of the fund. They look upon the remainder of the money in the fund as their own money, which actually it is. Since they have contributed into the fund moneys which are to be disbursed as assistance, they fail to see why the administration of that money should be put into the hands of non-farmers when farmers are available for that work. I do not know whether the department gives any instructions on that point to their field supervisors. If they do, I would hope that in future they would take the trouble to bring to the attention of the supervisors that where it is possible-that would be the case in probably 99 per cent of the districts-to engage the services of actual farmers to do the inspection work, that should be done. Only where such personnel is not available should they use other persons. Can the parliamentary assistant tell us whether any instructions are given in the first place to their supervisors as to the method they shall use in engaging their help? In the second place, are any instructions given to the effect that farmers should have the preference in filling these positions?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: REFERENCE TO STATEMENT BY DEPUTY POSTMASTER GENERAL RESPECTING ROBBERIES

They are to hire farmers or municipal men or men qualified to do this type of work. The farmer gets the preference in all cases.

subtopic: REFERENCE TO STATEMENT BY DEPUTY POSTMASTER GENERAL RESPECTING ROBBERIES

There are two sides to this thing. So far as the farmers are concerned, they are not always available to do it.

subtopic: REFERENCE TO STATEMENT BY DEPUTY POSTMASTER GENERAL RESPECTING ROBBERIES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I think the Prairie Farm Assistance Act is perhaps one of the most confusing pieces of legislation we have. When it was first set up it dealt almost entirely with drought conditions and there was no particular problem in designating areas that were eligible for benefits, but when it was extended to cover varying hazards it became more confusing. I have had interviews with the officials in Edmonton and in Ottawa and I want to pay my tribute to these fine fellows because they were most courteous and co-operative. They did everything within their power to find answers which would satisfy these people who were so worried.
[Mr. Welr.l
I come from what might be considered a new part of the country. I suppose it could be called a fringe area and we have special problems, which are not like those faced by what could be termed the dried-out areas. The people there do not seem to know anything about how the act applies to them and they feel that there is a certain amount of discrimination prevailing. There is a lot of confusion and misunderstanding and I should like to offer some suggestions to the minister.
I suggest that the minister consider putting out something in the form of a poster couched in simple terms which the average individual could understand. For instance it could set out what constitutes an eligible area, what would be the benefits accruing, and why certain areas are ruled out. These things are confusing to the people. For instance, they do not understand why they are denied benefits which their neighbours are getting. I know that there is a good reason for everything, but this seems to be a sore point in our part of the country.
Another question raised by these people is in connection with land taken since 1940. I appreciate the fact that when the ruling with regard to land of this type was brought into effect it was intended basically to deal with submarginal land. I think it was a good thing because it is anything but sensible for people to set themselves up as a going concern in places where the soil is not good. I think the reason for the ruling was wise, but the areas in our part of the country which were ruled out were not ruled out because of the lack of fertility of the soil. They were ruled out because they were considered to be located in places where a problem was posed, first of building roads and, second, of providing school facilities. For that reason they had to rule them out and they did not permit that land to be settled.
But what was a good thing 15 years ago is something different today. There has been rapid expansion in that part of the country and these areas now represent going concerns from a farming point of view. The land has been settled gradually, roads have been built, schools have been provided and crops are being produced which are normal when compared with those produced in any other community. But when adversity strikes they find that they are ruled out because of a technicality. I suggest that when the legislation is reviewed that matter be taken into consideration. I think it could be adjusted to do what it was intended to do in the first place and provide a service to these people which would be satisfactory.

There are other things which I would like to say but I do not want to take up the time of the committee in saying them. I ask the minister to consider this idea of putting out a poster which could be put up in the rural post offices where everyone could see it. If anyone felt he had a claim he could go and look at the rules of the game and then decide what he wanted to do. That would save a lot of money and it would enhance the good will that should prevail between the Department of Agriculture and the producer. Administrative costs would be reduced, as many of these questions could be simply and easily answered by putting out true facts in understandable terms. I do not think there is one man in a dozen who can take this act with its technical phraseology and understand what it is all about. The average man may be able to interpret part of it, but when it comes to interpreting the whole act, that is more than he can do. This suggestion, I think, is a reasonable one which would pay dividends in many ways.

subtopic: REFERENCE TO STATEMENT BY DEPUTY POSTMASTER GENERAL RESPECTING ROBBERIES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I want to say one final word in respect to this act and to repeat my plea that a change be made in the method of calculation for prairie farm assistance to the basis of the individual farm unit. I know this matter has been brought to the attention of the minister before and it may be considered that it is superfluous for me to bring it up at this time, but I do so because of what has occurred during the past year in a particular area in my constituency.
I know it is argued that to administer this act on the basis of the individual farm unit would be akin to a crop insurance plan and that the act was not essentially such a plan but rather a sort of farm relief plan whereby the farmer would be able to remain on his farm and pay the few essential expenditures in order to tide him over to the next crop year.
Mr. Chairman, the minister has also stated that if such an act was to be considered as a crop insurance act he might meet with some constitutional difficulties. I just cannot accept that reasoning. I do not believe there are any constitutional difficulties that would stand in the way, and I do not see why it cannot be administered on the basis of the farmer's need when, through drought or through some other unforeseen circumstances within the meaning of the act, he himself has lost his crop. Under the present system there just is not justice given having regard to the needs of these farmers who find they end a crop year without a crop.
I have mentioned this matter before. The minister knows all about it. Hon. members
Supply-Agriculture
here know all about it. But can we emphasize too much the injustice that is done to a farmer who is hailed out? Suppose he is in a long strip of hail storm. Suppose he is hailed out or is dried out and receives a yield which should ordinarily bring him within the meaning of the act so that he can get payment. But because he is not in a certain block of sections the yield of which is higher than his, he cannot receive payment. Yet his neighbour right across the road, whose yield is higher than his, receives the prairie farm assistance payment. You cannot tell the man who has received a lesser yield that there is any justice in an act which gives payment to his neighbour who received a bigger yield. There is no arguing around that point. You cannot get away from the argument that such a circumstance is indeed unjust. The farmer with the lower yield has paid into the fund over the years, and he has perhaps paid more into the fund than has his neighbour across the road whose yield is bigger but who yet receives the prairie farm assistance payment.
Let me suggest, Mr. Chairman, to the parliamentary assistant, to the minister and to the government that there is one principle we must remember in the bringing into operation of any legislation and it is this. No act is worth a great deal if those who are affected by the act have no confidence in it. The one thing that makes a piece of legislation sound is the fact that the people affected have confidence in the legislation. If there is anything that will destroy confidence in any legislation, it is when the administration of that legislation, although within the confines of the terms of the act, proves to be unjust. I cannot see that there can be any argument against that proposition.
I now come to just a bit of a grievance in respect to the particular section of the country which I have in mind. In presenting this grievance I would suggest to the minister that 1 am not complaining of the close and efficient attention which the top-level officials within the provinces are giving to the administration of this act, the responsibility for which is theirs wherever they may be located. In presenting certain complaints and individual cases to these top-level officials, I have always found that I have received commendable replies. Notwithstanding the fact that some hon. members may have criticism, I will say that I have always found them to be fair and that they have done their best to see if they could not remedy the complaint. However, I wish to support the hon. member for Dauphin who, speaking a little while ago on this matter, at least connoted that there may be a feeling that some inefficiency exists in respect of the lower level.

Supply-Agriculture
I refer to inspectors who went around attempting to solve the prairie farm assistance problems in certain areas.
The problem largely arises when a certain community or section of the country is passing through a year in which they have experienced conditions which had not previously occurred. Perhaps it is an area where they have had fair crops over the years. Perhaps they have not come under the act for years. Then suddenly a poor year strikes that community and a number of farmers in that section-perhaps a considerable number of them-are affected. Perhaps the unfortunate circumstances may be applicable to a large area. They now find themselves with a crop failure by reason of drought, hail or something else. So they begin to make application.
Municipal officials begin calculating and certain areas are determined as eligible areas. The inspectors are now sent in. If my information is correct, I am afraid that some of these inspectors have not been just as competent as they might have been in going into a new area. The result has led to considerable confusion.
For instance, certain information is required when a farmer makes application for payment. The inspector may go to him or he may call a number of farmers into town when he is there and he may take that information. Many farmers are obliged to rely upon their memory for statistics and they answer the questions to the best of their ability. The farmer signs his name to the application form which contains all the questions asked. That is all right. We have no complaint about that. But that form has often been regarded as absolutely final, even though the farmer perhaps has had to trust to his memory for a good deal of the information.
I have one instance in which farmers got together and began to compare notes afterwards, and in which they found they had given incorrect information. It was not done intentionally but through a slip of the mind; it was something they did not remember. Then upon making inquiries they found that the document they had signed was regarded almost as a sworn statement. Some of these farmers were told this: "You cannot change your mind now. If you do so, you may be subject to a charge of perjury".
That word "perjury" is a dynamic word. It strikes terror in the hearts of those who do not recognize all the implications which might be involved. Some farmers have said, "I am not going to run the risk of being put in jail," and so they let the matter go. I went to some of these farmers and I said to

them, "Have you that application that you signed?"; the answer I received was, "No; I have not. No copy was left with me".
I give this illustration in order to indicate that there can be some confusion in new areas of that kind where past records are not available. We know that when this act first came into existence there was tremendous confusion because farmers very often do not keep any-too-accurate records and they had to rely on their memories. As the years went by, in those areas which suffered more or less continually from drought, the government officials had the records there.
The farmers have learned to keep more accurate records. That problem is now largely solved but in new areas the same problems can exist. I want to say to the parliamentary assistant that I believe that one thing that should be impressed upon inspectors, as they go into an area in connection with the Prairie Farm Assistance Act, is that they should try as far as possible to satisfy the farmer and give any benefit of the doubt to the farmer who has perhaps paid into the fund for many years. The impression some farmers get is that the inspector is there to try to do them out of something that it is the farmers' right to receive. I am not going to say the inspectors do that, but that seems to be the general impression that some of the farmers in this particular area receive.
That is why I agree with members who have spoken previously that these inspectors should be men with some farm experience. I know that is not always possible but they at least should be men who have had experience with the act, who know what the act means, who are experienced enough to understand the farmer's problem and can sit down with the farmer as a friend and say to the farmer; "You have lost your crop and I am here to help you." They should take the information on that basis and there is no reason why a copy of the application and questionnaire should not be left with the farmer so that he will know exactly what he has signed. If he finds he has made a mistake he can make a complaint and have a review of his application on the basis of further information received.
I present this matter to the parliamentary assistant and ask him to pass it on to his minister and the appropriate officials so as to make certain that the farmers get what is actually coming to them if they find themselves in the unfortunate circumstances of losing a crop. Once again I urge that in order to make the act just and equitable in its application to the farmers we consider putting payments on an individual farm basis. I know it is said that would be a lot of work

but I do not believe it would involve any more administrative work than at the present time.
With respect to the suggestion that it would then be a crop insurance plan and might run into constitutional difficulties, I do not believe that is so. When a community is hard hit and relief comes into the picture the people go to their municipal officials. What do they say? They do not say that if a person lives on a certain street and in a certain block he cannot get assistance but has to live in a particular block that is regarded as eligible. They do not think of things in those terms. It is a case of whether the individual is in need. If this act is an act devised to tide the farmer over by reason of individual need because he has lost his crop, then he should be considered on the basis of his individual farm.
I propose that again and I say to the minister that I am going to keep on proposing it whenever I have the opportunity. I think all western members should do a little worrying of the minister. They should keep on worrying him, worrying him and worrying him until he turns around and says that something must be done. I will not take any more time of the committee. I do not think I will need to do so on any of the remaining items. This is the only item on which I have spoken and having done so I have a clear conscience now that I have presented the matter in the best and strongest way I can.
