speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am very glad to carry on in that way. I am not by any means-and I know the committee would not

expect me-going to make a review of the general international situation; but, as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has just said, there have been some recent important developments. Possibly I can mention them, all the more so because certain questions have been asked of me in the house in the last day or two and I said when my estimates came up I would deal with them.
Since I last spoke, indeed since I appeared before the committee on external affairs not very many weeks ago, the improvement in the international atmosphere has, I think it is fair to say, continued. There has been now for many months an easing of tension which has reflected itself in international meetings that have taken place recently. Whether this change-and I have said this before in the house-is merely a matter of tactics on the other side or whether it represents a change in long-range policy, I do not know. Nor do I think it would be wise to attempt to come to any conclusion on this matter. It would, I think, be premature to assume that the danger of conflict which has existed now between the two worlds for many years has been removed, or indeed sensibly decreased.
While we must be careful and must remain on guard, it would also be, I think, very shortsighted and unwise if we did not take advantage of every opportunity-and there have been opportunities recently-to broaden and deepen this improvement in the international situation which has taken place. In the Far East there has been some easing of tension. There has developed in a very dangerous part of the world now, the Formosa straits, what one might call a de facto ceasefire. Efforts have been made by governments not committed to either side in this world controversy, governments which have sometimes been called neutralists-I am thinking of the government of India and the government of Burma, and I am also thinking of the secretary general of the United Nations -efforts have been made to mediate certain outstanding differences that have for some time now persisted between the communist government of China and other governments, particularly the government of the United States. But that area of the Far East and the Formosa straits remains a danger area, and no one can rest easy as long as the two Chinese governments face each other in hard and bitter hostility, with forces at grips at and about the offshore islands, islands that are only a few miles off the coast of China.
In Europe the improvement in the atmosphere which I have been talking about has culminated this week in a meeting at the summit, as it is called, at Geneva, which

ended this afternoon. There were very great expectations and hopes aroused by this meeting of the heads of the four governments, and there will be those who will say that those hopes and those expectations have not been realized. But I think everyone who has been following the course of international events in recent years, and who has been guided by experience and not by emotion in these matters, must have realized from the time this meeting was called that it would be unrealistic to expect important developments out of one meeting at the summit, in the sense that problems would be solved and difficulties removed.
What has happened this week at Geneva- and I think this is something that might give us all cause for real satisfaction-is that problems have been identified, positions have been clarified and machinery has been set up for the diplomatic negotiation of those problems in the months ahead through the foreign ministers of the four great powers.
In that sense the Geneva meeting has been most valuable and encouraging. It has not solved the problems-and I myself never thought it would-but it has taken the first right step on what might become a road along which progress can be made in solving these problems. Any hon. member who has followed what has been going on at Geneva this week will, I know, be struck by the fact that while problems have been clarified to some extent, while machinery has been set up and views have been exchanged, the problems are still there. As far as I can gather there has not been very much alteration in the fundamental policies on the other side in respect of such things as the unification of Germany and the limitation of armaments.
What has happened is that the presentation of the case by the other side-I think we must all welcome this, especially those of us who have been subjected to the other type of presentation-has been more affable. That is all to the good. I think we can take some satisfaction at least from this change of atmosphere which may lead to something more important now that the process of negotiation has begun. Personally I hope for a continuation of this process through the foreign ministers and through other mechanisms inside and outside of the United Nations which may be set up or which have already been set up. I hope that in this process the negotiators will not be subjected to such publicity, exciting publicity, as that which has been reflected by the presence at Geneva this week of between 1,500 and 2,000 press, radio and television correspondents. I agree, however, that on this particular occasion at a meeting held at the summit one can expect that kind of attention.
Supply-External Affairs
In other words, what has happened at Geneva is the beginning of a long process which we hope will in the end result in the solution of some of the problems that divide the world, which if they are not solved will result in danger to all. No one meeting at the summit will solve these problems. A multitude of meetings below the summit, official and non-official, will be required. That process has begun and we are hoping that it will be satisfactorily concluded. It will require, on our side, patience and strength and unity.
Before the Geneva meeting began, just a week ago today, I had the privilege of attending a meeting of the NATO council in Paris at which the 15 foreign ministers of the NATO governments were present. At that meeting -I think this is the process of consultation at its best; it is one of the things we hoped NATO would be used for-the three foreign ministers who were going to Geneva told those representing the other 12 member states quite frankly and quite fully their hopes and their fears about Geneva, their plans and their policies, and gave us an opportunity to express our views.
In no sense did those three act at Geneva for the other 12, as we had our responsibilities to our own parliaments and governments. They could not, of course, be delegated by a NATO council meeting in Paris. But that meeting did give us a chance to hear of their plans and policies, to comment on them, to give them our own views. In that sense it was valuable. It was also an interesting and useful indication of the unity of the countries making up the NATO coalition. On the eve of the Geneva conference I think that may have been wise and of some value because the Geneva discussions have shown that one of the primary objectives of the Soviet union and its friends is to weaken, or indeed to break up, that coalition. That is why I said last Saturday in Paris that NATO was not negotiable.
When I said that I did not mean that the deployment, the level of armaments, or the uses to which forces could be put and all that sort of thing were not negotiable. It may be part of the general price we will have to pay for a true peace settlement. That sort of thing can be discussed with anybody at NATO or outside of NATO. But NATO itself as a regional organization for collective security is not negotiable; its existence is not up for negotiation as long as there is no better way through the United Nations to guarantee our security collectively.
At London before and after the NATO meeting I had the opportunity to discuss

Supply-External Affairs developments with the foreign minister and other members of the United Kingdom government.
While I have mentioned the Geneva conference and NATO I would not want to overlook one other useful meeting in recent weeks, the meeting at San Francisco to celebrate the tenth anniversary of the United Nations. I think that meeting turned out to be a very good and valuable development because it focused, and there was need to focus at this time, the attention of the world on the United Nations and its achievements about which we do not always hear so much, as well as its failures about which we always hear more; about its limitations as well as its possibilities.
The words used most often in the 72 speeches to which we listened at the San Francisco conference-71 in my case, because I made one myself-were "stocktaking" and "rededication". We took stock of the past and we looked to the future. Practically without exception, and this also applies to the delegations from the other side of the iron curtain, every statement ended with an expression of support for the United Nations as the indispensable and universal agency for the solution of disputes and the removal of difficulties, as the indispensable agency for international co-operation.
If it could only do the work it was meant to do ten years ago when we set it up we would not be talking today about NATO or conferences at the summit, because we would not need them. It may be that one day we will be able to use that world organization as it was meant to be used. Until that time we will be well advised, in so far as political collective security is concerned, to continue our support for regional organizations like the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, to keep them strong and united, to do our very best to convince those who fear these organizations that they are defensive in character, that they have no aggressive intent against anybody. If conditions improve, if there is more trust and confidence in the world than unfortunately is now the case, then, but only then, we will be able to modify our attitude toward these regional defensive collective organizations, especially if the work which they now do can be done through the United Nations.
On the whole, then, I would say that the last two or three months have given us cause not for exultation, not for unreasonable expectation, but for sober encouragement. The processes of negotiation between the two worlds have now begun. Some imaginative proposals have been put forward, especially the one by the President of the United States


the day before yesterday in respect to disarmament. That is a key subject, as it has been for many years, and it is an evidence of our good intentions.
All this has been hopeful and has been helpful. If we can continue on our side that process which we have begun, not merely relying on our strength and our unity but also on our determination to achieve the one objective which matters most in the hydrogen age, namely peace; if we subordinate everything to that objective and maintain a realistic sense of balance, not being too excited or encouraged when things seem to go right- sometimes dramatically so-and not getting too depressed or downcast when things seem to be going wrong; and if we can maintain the essential unity with our friends which we have built up over these years, then I think we can look forward to the immediate future with more confidence than we could a year ago today.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this statement by the Secretary of State for External Affairs at the opening of the discussion of the estimates of his department will be welcomed by the members of this house for several reasons. One is that we had already been informed that a statement would be made at this time when a reference to the proposals at Geneva had been made a few days ago. The other is the fact that it provides the opportunity to bring us up to date with regard to these international discussions upon which, in a large measure, all our hopes must depend.
It is not our intention to discuss the estimates at any length. The estimates were referred to a committee and they have been discussed extensively before that committee. Without suggesting that all matters relating to these estimates have been dealt with to our satisfaction, it is a fact that the opportunity to discuss them has been presented in that way, and we have indicated our belief that great advantage will be obtained if the estimates of all departments can be discussed in the same way as much as possible.
I wish to make reference to some statements made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs, because it seems to me that in these dramatic days of the present week there may have been, on the one hand, a danger of too great hopes of great achievement with regard to the issues that are so important to all of us and, on the other hand, some tendency to be discouraged too readily by the failure to present any positive form of statement that there is a solution of any of these great problems. It is only necessary to point out that under our system of government it is not possible for the government of Britain, the United States or France to reach

final conclusions at a meeting of this kind. The proposals that were put forward-and some of them were dramatic in their possibilities-would have gone back to the legislative bodies of the different countries for consideration and approval in any event.
It does seem that the most striking suggestion that was made, and one which has caught the imagination of the people throughout the world generally, was the suggestion by President Eisenhower the day before yesterday that in addition to the blueprints showing the disposition of defence production and arrangements, there should be afforded an opportunity to fly over the different countries where preparations are being made and in that way examine the country itself, as people have come to examine the ground from the air, to confirm the information already received.
I do not think there is anything unduly startling about that proposition. Anything short of that procedure would not be effective in any general plan of disarmament. Anything that did not ensure full information might, in fact, be only a trap and might invite one country or one group of nations to disarm in good faith while a nation that had aggressive tendencies might do the very opposite. It does indicate, however, that on this occasion, as the Secretary of State for External Affairs has pointed out, the heads of state of the four nations have discussed their problems in an atmosphere which seemed to produce a more satisfactory exchange of ideas than has occurred for many years.
The meeting terminated this afternoon, as has already been mentioned. There have been definite decisions. One of the definite decisions was that there will be a meeting of the foreign ministers in Geneva next October to consider problems of German unification and European security. That in itself is a positive achievement. At the discussions which took place it became clear that German reunification is the No. 1 problem which must be dealt with. Unquestionably it is associated with European security and, in fact, with all security.
Another positive decision that was reached before adjournment today was the reference to the United Nations subcommittee on disarmament of a series of disarmament proposals; and the subcommittee of the United Nations on disarmament was called on to meet in New York on August 29 to proceed with this work.
These are positive and definite decisions by this gathering of heads of state at the summit. The foreign ministers were directed 50433-422J
Supply-External Affairs to study the results of the proposed disarmament negotiations and to seek ways to bring about progressive elimination of barriers between the east and the west. As Canada is a member of the subcommittee along with Britain, the United States, France and Russia we are, of course, immediately brought into the results of these positive decisions.
This afternoon the Prime Minister of Britain expressed what undoubtedly must be a very general opinion throughout the world, when he said that these big four talks at the summit have brought about a better climate than that prevailing at any time since the second world war for proceeding to work effectively on proposals to solve east-west differences which have been dividing the nations. In the closing session President Eisenhower of the United States said this:
The prospects of a lasting peace with justice, well-being and broader freedom are brighter and the dangers of the overwhelming tragedy of modern war less.
Marshal Bulganin made the longest of the closing speeches, and said the Soviet union was disappointed that some topics which were of importance to them had not been raised. These include Asia, the Far East and the red Chinese bid for a seat in the United Nations, as well as discussion of the Formosa question. Premier Faure of France said the spirit which governed the debates and the mutual understanding which resulted will leave the brightest mark on international relations and will have a happy influence on their evolution.
These were positive statements made today by these men who have met in an atmosphere of friendliness and in a manner which certainly has not been common in recent years at meetings of representatives of these nations. President Eisenhower, in welcoming the spirit of friendliness in the speeches of Marshal Bulganin and Prime Minister Eden, who preceded him, did say that he hoped his silence respecting certain statements of Marshal Bulganin would not be interpreted as acquiescence on his part with any of those statements. I mention that particularly because I think as we discuss these subjects, which now will become subjects for discussion by representatives of the Canadian government and particularly the Secretary of State for External Affairs, we should remember that there were very important silences in the meeting at Geneva that has just ended.
One of the subjects that can never, I think, be disregarded, is the whole principle of security. The No. 1 question placed before the conference at Geneva was German unification. Russia emphasized that there must

Supply-External Affairs be European security before there could be talk of German unification. I submit that at this time, when we are discussing a subject that will be reviewed well before we meet again by the Secretary of State for External Affairs speaking on behalf of the Canadian government, we should point out something that emerges so clearly, the lesson of what happened after the first world war. That lesson is that problems are not solved by disregarding them.
When we talk about European security I think it is important that we remember that other terms of security have also been discussed. The extent to which any arrangement for European security is going to carry conviction and confidence to the governments of the nations of the earth, as well as the people behind those governments, will depend upon the measure of frankness with which the arrangements for security already made have been carried into effect. For that reason I think we must go back to the meeting in San Francisco this year commemorating the tenth anniversary of the signing of the charter of the United Nations. The Secretary of State for External Affairs has said that whatever hopeful results there may have been from this meeting, the problems still remain.
I submit that we would be unrealistic in discussing German unification and terms of European security unless we remember that terms of security affecting many other nations were discussed at San Francisco ten years ago. The Secretary of State for External Affairs has said, and properly so, that we should be guided by experience and not by emotion. The natural desire to accept the good that has come from these meetings should not hide from us certain realities that have not yet been faced. The Secretary of State for External Affairs has told us that at San Francisco this year two words that were constantly repeated were "stocktaking" and "rededication". That is right.
I dislike appearing to stress over and over again something that seems to me fundamental in any discussion of security and international relations at this time. If we do make an honest stocktaking of the international situation we surely must start with the acceptance of the reality that in spite of the assurance at San Francisco in June of 1945 that the nations which were signing the charter, including Russia, were joined in the desire to preserve the integrity of international boundaries and the self-determination of nations, we now see scores of millions of people enslaved throughout the world by Russian aggression, contrary to the declaration in the charter of the United Nations in

1945. That is one reality that is part of the stocktaking that must precede any frank discussion of European or other security.
We should remember that this was no general inclusion of broad terms of national self-determination. A few months earlier, in February of 1945, Stalin had given a solemn undertaking that the countries in Europe occupied by the Russian armies would be permitted to choose their own governments by free elections. That principle was reasserted in the charter of the United Nations signed at San Francisco on June 26, 1945. Those pledges have been violated by Russia. Yet they were recognized at that time as the very foundation of any plan for national security.
I submit, Mr. Chairman, that if there is one message that should go to the Secretary of State for External Affairs from this house prior to his discussion of these subjects in New York in August, it is that the stocktaking should include that reality. How can the people of one part of Europe place greater faith in agreements for national security than the people of other parts of Europe? If Poland, the Baltic states, Czechoslovakia, Roumania, Hungary and the other nations now under Russian control find the undertakings given by Russia ten years ago utterly valueless, then what reason have any other nations adjoining them to have more confidence that the terms of any agreement made today will be carried out?
I submit that this is the time to ask our government to point out at the meeting of the United Nations subcommittee in New York in August that along with any discussion of European security there should be a stocktaking in regard to the security or lack of security of those nations which were promised free elections by the head of the Russian government in 1945. I do not see how any assurances given today can have any real sanction unless those undertakings are carried out.
I think we should say, as Canadians, that this subject is part and parcel of any general plan of security. Does the freedom of the people of Poland, of the people of the Ukraine, and all those other countries that were promised free votes by the solemn pledge of the head of the Russian government, mean nothing to us? Are we less concerned about those promises than about other promises? We were also parties to the charter of the United Nations, signed at San Francisco. If we must tag some promises which are to be regarded as solemn and others which are to be regarded as not so solemn, then where does security begin and where does security end?

The Secretary of State for External Affairs has repeated a statement he made about NATO not being negotiable. I believe that was a very apt statement. I think we might well say that freedom is not negotiable. I believe we must decide, as we thought the nations had decided at San Francisco in 1945, that freedom is indivisible. If we are prepared to negotiate the terms of freedom and disregard our solemn promise on an earlier occasion that all nations would have this right, then I doubt the real sanction to the promises that would be made today. Canada, with the other nations, went to war in September, 1939, to support the principle that freedom is not divisible. It went to war in support of the principle that freedom is not negotiable. I think the gathering that will meet at the end of August in New York should reassert that principle and rededicate itself to the opening paragraph of the charter of the United Nations.
We should remember also that when we talk about terms of reunification we are talking about the most explosive subject that we can discuss today. I do not think there was any course open but to agree to the rearmament of Western Germany, but we should recognize that the moment we agreed to that we accepted the full consequences of that rearmament. Germany has made such a recovery as no nation has made in all history. Out of the ashes they have emerged as the most dynamic industrial power in continental Europe at this time. Now they will begin to devote that tremendous industrial energy to the production of arms. They will start from scratch. In doing so they will have all the advantages of the developments the western nations have devised in the way of weapons. From past experience we can be confident that it will not be very long before Germany will be improving upon the designs placed at her disposal, and that once again there will be weapons of the greatest power emerging from German workshops.
What happens then? What happens five years from now, six years at the outside, when a rearmed Western Germany looks to Eastern Germany which will be still under Russian control if there has not been unification at that time? Can anyone doubt the temptation there will be for Germany to seek reunification under other terms than those which are explicit in the Paris agreements signed a few months ago? I am confident Chancellor Adenauer intends to carry out this agreement, but Chancellor Adenauer is not immortal. Some other chancellor may be called upon to make decisions. Let us remember that at this stage after the first world war Stresemann was head of the German government. There
Supply-External Affairs was a democracy in Germany and the Weimar republic was showing every sign of carrying democracy into action. It was not many years later that the democracy which had promised so much had disappeared under a nazi government, with all the terror and all the horrors that followed.
These things must be faced today; the unification of Germany and a definition of what we mean by the unification of Germany, whether it merely includes the unification of Western Germany with the present eastern zone or something more. Those are things to decide at this stage, and not leave unsettled until Germany has regained more military power. Another lesson that emerges from history is that any nation which develops a dynamic military and industrial expansion is not likely to stop that development no matter what the limitations may be. This is the time, therefore, to reach agreement on what reunification means, and also to reassess the situation; to have a real stocktaking, and to be sure that no terms of international security in Europe or elsewhere are going to inspire too much confidence unless the basic promise of national self-determination contained in the charter of the United Nations is reasserted by nations which have truly dedicated themselves to what was undertaken at that time.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs has said that there should be patience, strength and unity. We will all agree with those terms. I think also there must be, as he has said, a stocktaking, but a stocktaking which in all reality faces the situation that is before us. Then having taken stock we should seek to base our plans for the future upon the real undertakings of the United Nations Organization, which offers the one real hope of peace to this world today.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
We in this group, Mr. Chairman, welcome the statement made today by the Secretary of State for External Affairs. With him, with all members of this house, and with Canadians generally we welcome what has taken place in Geneva this week. We recognize that the basic problems facing our world have not been settled at Geneva, but it is true that some of these problems have been faced, have been identified and have been referred to the appropriate bodies for further study. Even on that score we think there has been progress at Geneva this week.
However, like the Secretary of State for External Affairs we feel that perhaps the most important result of the meeting at the summit has been an improvement in the international climate. To use the minister's own words, even if there has been only an improvement

Supply-External Affairs in affability that is something to welcome. We are glad the four heads of state were at last able to get together; and we believe there is reality and substance in the improved climate that seems to have resulted from these important meetings.
Somehow or another it seems to me that the most important development of this past week, or of the past several weeks-because the meetings at the summit involved more than a week; they involved also weeks of preparation for those meetings-is the realization that seems to have come over those in high places that in this atomic and hydrogen world we simply have to find a way to avoid war. To us it is highly significant that the statement signed by the late Albert Einstein, and the group of scientists, happened to be made just before the meetings at Geneva were held. And it does seem to us that the warning given to us by those scientists had some effect on the thinking of those who met at Geneva, and on the discussions that took place.
We recognize that the world's problems still exist. We recognize that we must remain on guard. Nevertheless, it seems to me the Secretary of State for External Affairs was justified in being hopeful in what he said today. It is the task of those of us who speak in public, either here or elsewhere, those of us who have the task of giving leadership to our people in this country, to try to push forward that hopeful attitude. It seems to me that the idea held by the man in the street, the idea that somehow in this day and age it is not just a case of who can win the next war but rather that the next war must be avoided, has found expression officially at the highest possible level. Therefore, we think we have a right to be hopeful, as a result of the meetings which have taken place this week.
I should like to say, in the same vein, that we are glad to know that if he can arrange it the Secretary of State for External Affairs intends to pay a visit to the Soviet union some time before the year is out. We hope also the government will give favourable consideration to the idea of exchanges of visits between various people in that country and this. I place emphasis on the word "exchanges" because it seems to me it is desirable not only that more members of parliament and more Canadians generally should have a chance to visit that country, but also highly desirable that we persuade delegations from the Soviet union to visit our country. Surely it is axiomatic that if we can get to know each other better, whether through meetings of heads of states or through ordinary people seeing each other and each other's countries, it will further the 

cause of mutual understanding and help to get rid of some of the fears that have bedevilled our world for such a long time.
We were pleased by the imaginative suggestion put forward by President Eisenhower at Geneva a couple of days ago. Whether or not that suggestion in its exact terms is carried out, we hope there will be a very serious and determined effort on behalf of all nations to get rid of the fears and misunderstandings which have divided us in the years since the end of world war II.
So, as I have already indicated, we welcome this improved climate, this better atmosphere. We believe it is the job of the minister, the job of all of us, to take advantage of that improved climate and do nothing that will throw any clouds in the way, but rather to do our best to further the cause to which the Secretary of State for External Affairs referred in his closing words, the cause of peace.
Perhaps it is highly significant, when one talks about a change in atmosphere, that we have come once again to a time when we can use the word "peace" without having to apologize. I think hon. members know what I have in mind when I say that. Surely that is our objective. Surely the frightening prospect of what atomic or hydrogen war would do to mankind makes us realize that peace must be our objective, if we are to remain alive. And it may be that out of this will come the possibility of our doing more than just keeping civilization alive, the possibility of using the tremendous forces now at our disposal to lift civilization to a higher standard of security and well-being than we have yet known.
We were also pleased that the Secretary of State for External Affairs made the reference he did to the meetings held at San Francisco commemorating the tenth anniversary of the United Nations. Certain jocular remarks were made about those meetings before they were held, particularly in the committee on external affairs, suggesting that the meetings would be a bit boring, that they would consist of just a succession of speeches by delegates representing the various member states. In fact, the meetings were very interesting. It was significant that the radio and television networks gave such extensive coverage to those meetings, and that people were glad to listen to and watch the proceedings at San Francisco on this important occasion.
I wholly endorse the minister's statement that it was good at this time to hold these meetings and thereby to focus attention on the United Nations. For, after all, I believe it is fair to say that the government regards

the United Nations as the cornerstone of Canada's foreign policy. Our hope for peace, our hope for avoiding atomic or hydrogen war, and our hope for a higher standard of security and well-being for our people depend, in the long run, not on regional pacts, necessary though they may be under certain conditions, but rather upon the achievement of a system of universal collective security.
We accept the position taken by the Secretary of State for External Affairs today with regard to the present necessity of regional pacts such as NATO. But I was very pleased to hear him say that if we can strengthen the United Nations to the point where it offers the kind of security we want, it will. be possible to modify our attitude toward regional pacts. It seems to me those were very important words used by the minister this afternoon; and we in this group urge the government to do everything it possibly can to strengthen the United Nations to the end that the day might come, and come soon, when we will have a greater degree of universal collective security than we have at the present time.
Not only do we feel that support for the United Nations, which the government affirms to be the cornerstone of its foreign policy, should be pursued with respect to security arrangements, but we also feel very strongly that all possible support should be given to the various specialized agencies, the various social and humanitarian programs which are sponsored under the United Nations.
I know the government will say this is its policy and its practice, and we are prepared to commend the government on the extent to which it supports bodies like the world health organization, the international labour organization, and many others which are related to the economic and social council of the United Nations. But I think it is fair to say that we still have a long way to go in developing our aid programs, putting them on the kind of basis that will really remove the causes of war and help to share the possibility of a decent life amongst all the peoples of the world.
I for one-and I am sure others feel the same way-was impressed by the remarks made before the committee on external affairs by an outstanding Canadian, Dr. H. L. Keenleyside, who is now the director general of the United Nations technical assistance administration. It was a very moving story that Dr. Keenleyside was able to tell us of what this administration has been able to do. And yet, despite the careful and diplomatic way in which Dr. Keenleyside presented the case, there was clear there between the lines his feeling that a lot more could be done
Supply-External Affairs if only more money were available from all countries that belong to the United Nations. In this house we have a great deal of respect for the opinion and the judgment of Dr. Keenleyside, and we feel that what he said with regard to the United Nations technical assistance program should be given serious consideration; and this applies also to the Colombo plan and to other plans of this type.
We would like to stress once again our belief that a great deal could be done for the cause of world peace by increasing the exchange of students, by bringing to this country more people from the underdeveloped parts of the world, so we might impart to them the skills and the abilities that we have learned in this country. These things have become trite, Mr. Chairman. They are recognized as truisms. But so often we do not pay the attention we might to things that are axiomatic.
There is an element of real urgency about this. Time is of the essence. If we really want to achieve the goal stated by the Secretary of State for External Affairs, namely that of subordinating everything to the objective of peace, we feel we have to get down to the basic underlying economic causes of world unrest. Yes, Canada is doing a great deal. Yes, I know there are Canadians -and all of us have received letters of this kind-who suggest that we should be doing certain things here at home before we give money or other things to people in other lands. Entirely apart from the moral or ethical principles involved in such a program, I suggest it is basic to the cause of peace that we greatly increase our efforts to help raise the living standards, economic security and social well-being of the world around us.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, because we have had many discussions this session on external affairs, both in the House of Commons itself and in the committee on external affairs, we do not feel it is necessary to extend our remarks at this time. But we welcome what has been said today by the Secretary of State for External Affairs, and we want him to know that so far as this group are concerned we want every effort put into the program he has laid before us today, namely that of subordinating everything to the objective of peace so that instead of the frightening, awful prospect of another war, we might look forward to a day of peace, security, well-being and abundance, not just for the people of Canada but for the people of all the world.
I am sure the minister agrees with us in this. There is no other way to achieve peace for ourselves than by achieving it for all mankind. Canada is in a very strong position

Supply-External Affairs to play a part in such a campaign. The minister will have our full support in everything he does to press forward a real campaign for peace.

Mr. Chairman, first I want to thank the minister for the statement he presented to the committee today, bringing us up to date on developments that have taken place in world affairs since last we had a chance to debate external relations.
The committee on external affairs, Mr. Chairman, did study quite thoroughly the estimates of the minister's department. We had every opportunity to question the minister and his officials about the details of the estimates. It will be remembered that during the year much time was spent by the committee on Bill No. 3, which gave many members a liberal course in hydrodynamics as well as in some other things. Since there was a pretty thorough study of the estimates, it would seem that at the present time there need not be a lengthy debate on external affairs.
There has been some change in the world situation since April, and the minister has indicated the change; but it does seem to me that change is not too significant. Well, at least it would not warrant a long speech on my part. I was interested in hearing the minister mention the improvement in the international atmosphere. He spoke of the easing of tension that had been reflected in the international meetings that have taken place of late, but he did realistically challenge the situation by saying we are not certain whether it indicates a change in tactics on the part of the other side, or whether it indicates the beginning of a change in long-range policy. Well, I too think it would be dangerous to assume that suddenly the Russians have abandoned their long-range policy. I do not think it would be wise at all for any of us to believe that the battle for men's minds will not go on unabated in spite of the fact that there have been some improvements in the international atmosphere.
This brings me to the four-power conference at Geneva. I cannot say, Mr. Chairman, that I looked forward to any great achievements as a consequence of that conference. We had our hopes, of course. We had our expectations, I suppose, the same as anyone else; but they were tempered by realism based on our experience in the past. It seems to me that about the only thing that could possibly come out of the Geneva conference at this time would be perhaps a little better opportunity for the application of some of the old style type of diplomacy, where the leaders would get together in an atmosphere


of friendliness, talk over the problems confronting the states of the world and perhaps lay the foundation for some of the understandings which we may not have had in the past. But, as I say, I am afraid I did not expect very much out of it. The minister says that machinery has been set up by the leaders of the four great powers which will carry on discussions in the months ahead. Probably something will be achieved, but he did state realistically that while the machinery was set up the problems were still there.
I was somewhat surprised two days ago when President Eisenhower made his proposal for a full exchange of blueprints of military establishments, and also full inspection methods on both sides. I wondered at the time whether it was based entirely on good will or whether there was not also some realism mixed up with it. I think perhaps President Eisenhower wants sincerely to lay the foundation for the kind of control of armaments, and perhaps even for disarmament, for which we have been hoping for a long time, but one could hardly be expected not to read into it some other possibility.
I wondered at the time if President Eisenhower might not have felt that the western powers stood to gain more than they would give. I wondered just how far Russian intelligence had succeeded in getting blueprints of what we have. Perhaps an exchange such as that suggested by President Eisenhower would not be giving them much they did not have already, and maybe would yield to us a lot that we did not have. If it were made with that end in view I suppose that it was pretty realistic. I am satisfied in my own mind that the Russians have known a lot more about what we were doing than perhaps some of us thought.
At any rate I have not felt at all pessimistic about the outlook. As other hon. members have said, I do believe the Geneva conference will doubtless pay dividends. I think in future we will be able to look back to it and say that it was at least another beginning of something that brought good to the nations of the world. I think at least the leaders themselves after these conferences will have removed some of the fear that may have bound them. I do not believe they are going to worry too much about Bertrand Russell and his party of scientists, whose statements were resurrected just before the conference. I think they have been generally realistic about things and have swept away a good many of the cobwebs that were built out of fear, and doubtless they will come forward now with some pretty realistic things.

It is my opinion that the western powers, during the past year and a half or two years especially, have won a major victory in the cold war. In my judgment they won it by standing together and rejecting successfully any attempts that were made by the other side to divide them on matters of policy. I think that was the term used by the minister and I believe it is a good term to use in speaking about those whom today we look upon as our adversaries. I do believe we have made considerable progress because we have stood together and have not let them divide us.
The minister suggested that in the days ahead we must go forward in patience, strength and unity. That is true, and we support him in that. We say to him, "Go to the conference in August; make your trip to Moscow this fall when it can be arranged; go into every negotiation you possibly can with the idea of continuing to promote good will abroad, but temper it with essential realism." The minister has not indicated in anything he said today that he is unrealistic about the world situation, and we support him in the attitude he has taken.
But I do think while we are promoting good will abroad in an effort to further improve the whole atmosphere and further ease the tension that exists, we must not lose sight of the price that might have to be paid if too many of us continue to be imbued with the idea of appeasement for averting war. I think it is all very well to go to all these international conferences and negotiations with a view to preventing war, but we must also remember what might be the cost of anything we might do on our side to prevent war. I would rather stand up and fight and be completely destroyed in an effort to retain my liberty than adopt an attitude toward the necessity of being ready to fight that might give my liberty away by default. I think that is the attitude we have to take.
The Russians are realistic, and we have to be realistic. I think many of our people have been just a bit soft in the head in the past several years since the end of world war II. We have been too much influenced by communist propaganda. We have become the victims of fear instead of being imbued with faith. It seems to me that it is about time we cut away all these cobwebs of fear so we can see realistically what we are up against. I do believe that if we go forward in faith, determined to preserve our liberties, determined to stand together in unity, we will not be activated by fear. If we go into any negotiations with the idea of averting war at all costs, then in my opinion we will be endangering ourselves and this nation and other nations as well.
Supply-External Affairs
I would suggest to the minister that he do everything he can in the name of Canada and the western powers to avoid war, but let us not take any steps which might lead to surrender. I think the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre raised an important point when he said we should be spending more time seeking out the causes of war and doing something about them. Little real effort has been made in the past 50 or 60 years in trying to find the real causes of war instead of the alleged causes. As a parliament and as individuals we should be spending as much time as we possibly can in studying deeply and finding out the causes of war and how those causes can be rooted out and eliminated. When we do that I feel certain we can remove all fear of war, but not until we go into it with determination to clear away those causes that might be found, let us say, in our selfishness, in our greed and determination to impose upon nations of the world our views with respect to trade. By that I mean the feeling that we must have a favourable balance of trade with other nations, and mugt impose upon them in trade treaties such things as the unconditional most favoured nation clause that does not give them a chance. I think we must get down to a study of these things and find out how far they cause international tension and destroy any good will we might have built up as a consequence of our efforts in international conferences.
I think it is necessary for us to continue to develop in strength. We must not let down. It seems to me that no easing of tension should justify any relaxation in our efforts to build ourselves up in strength so we can stand with the other western nations in an effort to present to the other side the most formidable unity. I would rather have them say, "Let us not go up against those fellows, because they are terrible" than say, "I do not know, but I think perhaps the best way to get at these fellows is just to scare them a little bit about atomic or hydrogen warfare, and then we can whip them".
I think we must present a terrible front. When I say "terrible" I mean one that presents the prospect of being terrible to any enemy who might think of coming up against us. They will not pick a fight with people who are strong, but they will certainly try to pick a fight quickly with those who are weak. We therefore stand with the minister in every effort he and his government may make to keep Canada strong and to help the other nations of the western world to be strong, and I refer to strength in every phase of our national and international existence.

Supply-External Affairs
In a speech with which I could agree as to almost every word, the Leader of the Opposition this afternoon spoke at some length about security and how the United Nations can fit into the whole program of security. I think there can be no serious talk of the United Nations doing the job that many millions of people have hoped it would be able to do until it is in a position to tackle the problem of security, with a view to bringing security not only to the big nations but also to those smaller nations that have been enslaved by the other side. I am thinking of such nations as Poland, Czechoslovakia, Bulgaria, the Ukraine and East Germany.
All those peoples and countries have been subjugated. Their present position indicates that the word of the communist nations just cannot be taken, that it does not mean much. Until they are ready to show a changed attitude toward those peoples and those countries and indicate that they are ready to negotiate for their security and their freedom, in a manner similar to that in which they negotiated with Austria, then it seems to me that the work of the United Nations will be somewhat fruitless in the field of security.
As has already been said by others, I believe the recent tenth anniversary meeting in San Francisco was a good thing. Focusing the attention of the world upon the United Nations was a good thing. Let us build up the feeling on the part of people everywhere that the United Nations can be made into the kind of agency that will eventually bring peace. Let us do that by all means. But at the same time let us be realistic about it. Let us look at the charter and see whether we cannot make in it some changes that will revitalize and rehabilitate the United Nations so it can become the type of organization we dream about.
I very much doubt that the United Nations assembly itself can ever really be the effective agency it ought to be until the representatives who go there are the representatives of the people instead of the representatives of governments of nations. The security council is a different thing, as are some of the other specialized agencies. But I should like to see at the United Nations assembly persons who are sent there by the peoples of the various countries of the world and who reflect the will, the desire, the aims and the hopes of those people rather than of just the governments themselves.
I have always felt the same way. I think I spoke in that same manner back in 1945, when the San Francisco charter was brought before the house for ratification. I feel that


sort of thing ought to govern our attitude toward the United Nations today. By all means let us do everything we can to build it into an agency that can really do an effective job in the international field.
We are happy, Mr. Chairman, to go along with the minister in his expressed desire to use patience, to go forward with the other western nations in unity, and to prepare for any negotiations from strength. We extend to him our good will in everything he undertakes to do along those lines.

May I ask you to call it six o'clock, Mr. Chairman.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at eight o'clock.

Mr. Chairman, like others I listened with interest this afternoon to the speech of the minister, and particularly to what he had to say about the meeting "at the summit" at Geneva. I think we would be more or less than human if we had not been a bit disappointed, notwithstanding the warnings we have had, including the wise warning from the minister himself about this time last week when he was in Paris. After all, since 1950 when Truman made what Churchill called the "valiant decision", we have had a good deal to encourage us, though we must also not forget the discouragements in Indochina and elsewhere. I suppose it was inevitable that we should allow our hopes to rise pretty high and, as I said, I think we would be either more or less than human today if we were not just a trifle disappointed.
But on the other hand we had better put that aside and think only of the encouraging signs. After all, as the minister has pointed out it is a step forward that on speaking of the Russians the word "affability" could be used. It is not a word I like much. However, it means courtesy, and that is a word I do like. Incidentally, I used to think that people like Ernest Bevin and others, who had to confer with the Russians in the days when a conference meant shouting at each other in vituperative terms, deserved some special kind of decoration for enduring what they had to endure. It must have been a tremendously pleasant change for those who were in Geneva this week to be able to talk to their counterparts in a civilized manner. I think Europe will also have taken note of the visit of the United States President and the British Prime Minister, not to speak of their ladies who evidently made their own considerable impression in Europe as well.

But I wish to say a word or two now on what the minister has called stocktaking. We are, I think, more or less reduced to the pedestrian level again. The minister has pointed out that as a result of what has taken place at Geneva, smaller and less importantlooking meetings will take place at which detailed advances can be made. Meantime we are back, as I say, at the pedestrian level, and I want to say a word or two about the United Nations because it seems to me from my small experience of it that it is in great danger of not being taken as seriously as it should.
We all remember what happened to the league of nations. I suppose it is fair to say that in the twenties and thirties we lost peace because we were bored with peace. Peace is a very dull thing when you are not in-what shall I say-a fever of apprehension about losing it. As I look back to the 1930's it is almost impossible not to give way to torture of the mind when one thinks of the occasions which were lost-in 1933 when Hitler came to power, in 1935 at the time of Abyssinia when so many nations played such an ignoble part, and I suppose most of all in 1936 when Hitler invaded the Rhineland. When we look back we know with virtual certainty that if there had been anyone with as much courage as Truman had in 1950 war would not have come, or at any rate would not have come in the way it did.
It is not worth pausing to torture our minds about the failure of the league, but I want to say a word about the United Nations. It seems to me it is more than ever important for it to move ahead on all fronts, not merely on the military front but on constructive lines. We know what they are. I am not going to take the time of the committee to dwell on them. We must go ahead, as the minister has said, with faith and hope; but I think it is tremendously important that the work of the United Nations should in every way possible be magnified. We failed in that regard with respect to the league. People were not interested in the league. Actually those who stood out in the community and tried to interest the ordinary voter in the league were almost made fun of. I can remember people like the late Sir Robert Falconer, president of the University of Toronto, the late N. W. Rowell, at one time Liberal leader in Ontario and subsequently minister in the union government, men who toiled at the task, but what thanks did they ever get? They were regarded almost as harmless cranks.
As I say, people were in effect bored with peace. They would not take any trouble about it, and so they lost it. Now we have
Supply-External Affairs the United Nations, and in one way you might say that the task of the United Nations is even harder because of the new and overwhelming dangers which face us. But on the other hand there is a hope that these new and overwhelming dangers may actually have the effect of making people at last wake up to the fact that peace is in danger, so they will try to do something about it.
I have one practical suggestion I wish to make about the United Nations. I was fortunate enough to be there a year ago last autumn and, I imagine like many other people who were there, I had two feelings. First of all, that never in all my life had I seen so much frustration, with committees meeting and reporting morning after morning after morning and really having nothing to report. On the other hand, I had the feeling that if this institution had not existed it should be invented at once, for the reason that it was worth while to keep a place going where the nations of the world could come and talk to each other and, haply, find out how to avoid dropping bombs on each other.
It is in that connection I have one practical suggestion to make. It seemed to me that the meetings of the United Nations suffered greatly from the fact that not many of the top flight people were there, or if they were there it was just "how do you do" and "good-bye". If my feeling as to the importance of the United Nations is not exaggerated- and perhaps it is keener today than it would have been if there had been greater success at Geneva-then we should be doing more about it than we are. I am not overlooking the fact that the news and radio services give us very good news coverage, but it is my opinion that somehow or other we have to make the ordinary citizen understand more about it, and personally I cannot think of anything more likely to do that than having the important people go there.
With all the burdens that are on the Prime Minister, with all the important duties he has, I cannot believe there is anything more important than for him to make the occasional visit to the United Nations. It is only a matter of a few hours. As for the Secretary of State for External Affairs, who I know has had a great deal to do with the United Nations and is highly regarded there, he has many duties to perform and it would be a bold man who would ask him to do more unless we were able to divide him into two or three instead of being one and indivisible. But I do suggest to him the importance of having the United Nations regarded as a place of more importance than it is now. I suggest to him that it is a top priority task,
