Supply-External Affairs and in view of all the tasks the United Nations has to do and the vast importance of the part it can play if it attains the status it should attain, I put this forward as a practical suggestion for his consideration.

Mr. Chairman, I am unable to share the views expressed by the hon. member for Greenwood and the Leader of the Opposition who seem to have been disappointed with the results of the meeting at the summit. I am sure no one expected that all the problems of the world would be solved this past week. I think it is significant and encouraging that this meeting has taken place. A year ago very few of us expected that within a year it would have been possible for this meeting to have been held. I think we have to reach the conclusion very soon that either we have to fight the Russians or we have to live in the same world with them. Very few people in their right senses consider that we are going to fight the Russians. If we are not, I think we have to explore the field of conciliation, even although there are many difficult situations to solve.
The hon. member for Lethbridge, has indicated that he is not speaking unless there is some fool speech made this evening. While some of my speeches might be in that category, I am sure my remarks tonight will not be described by him in that way. I have two points I want to make. Something over a year ago, when the Prime Minister was making his tour of the world, I suggested he should include a visit to Moscow. The suggestion was accepted by the Prime Minister in the spirit in which it was given, but he was not able to change his plans. This suggestion received very favourable comment in the Canadian papers.
Later I suggested that since the Prime Minister could not go, the minister of external affairs should arrange a visit some time and take with him the Leader of the Opposition, the leader of our group, the leader of the Social Credit group and some other members of the house. I am very glad that while the minister is not arranging to take a group with him, he is arranging to visit Moscow before the end of the year.
We all feel that on the whole the Canadian Secretary of State for External Affairs has done an outstanding job throughout the years.
I think the members of all political parties feel that although he has been subject to criticism by the Russians and he has been criticized by Senator McCarthy, somewhere in between these two conflicting views the minister must have some virtues.
So far as Canada is concerned, we feel that we should be able to make a worth-while


contribution in this world of strain. For more than a hundred years we have been able to live with our immediate neighbour without any wars. We have never thought of establishing provincial armies. People from a great many countries have come to Canada and have been able to build up a pride in our common objectives. We have a long connection with Great Britain and with France. We have two very powerful neighbours, Russia to the north and the United States to the south. With our various attributes and with our strategic position, I think we should accept the challenge which is ours and make the best contribution possible.
Before this item passes I should like the minister to make some report to us on the suggestion made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre regarding an exchange of visitors. While the minister was away there was an editorial in the Toronto Globe and Mail, reprinted in the Ottawa Citizen of July 19, which is very brief. It says:
Why so solemn about Russians?
Need we really be so precise, so solemn, so anxious, in our dealings with Russia? Have we no sense of humour or self-confidence where that country is concerned? The supreme soviet has offered, in effect, to send a group of its members to Canada. Let Canada's parliament accept the offer, if only out of curiosity to see what Russian parliamentarians look like. And let it, in return, send a group of its own members to Russia.
We do not see how such visits can do anybody a particle of harm. And it is possible, at least, that over a period they might do some good. Such possibilities, in today's world, are all we have to work with. We should learn to use them with wisdom, with patience, and not least with good nature.
I think the time has now arrived when the Secretary of State for External Affairs should indicate to the house whether Canada could not accept this invitation in good faith and proceed to make the necessary arrangements. I know it is an unusual invitation. We have a NATO organization and we have a commonwealth parliamentary association, but we do not seem to have an organization in our parliament to deal with this particular sort of invitation. I think the Secretary of State for External Affairs might indicate whether or not Canada should accept or reject this invitation. In my view, and in the view of the editorial writer of the Globe and Mail, this invitation might be accepted.
The other point I want to raise is in connection with the need for an information section in the minister's department to deal particularly with the work of the United Nations and the specialized organizations. On several occasions I have mentioned the difficulty I have had in getting information concerning what is being done by FAO, WHO

or ILO. The minister's very efficient information office refers me to the Department of Agriculture or national health and welfare, if it is a health problem. When I get to national health and welfare and the minister is out of the city, the officials of that department refer me back to external affairs. If it is a Colombo plan problem they refer me to Mr. Cavell's department, and if Mr. Cavell is out of the city I am referred back to external affairs.
I think we need to recognize that while in Canada there is not any very serious opposition to the work of the United Nations or the specialized agencies of the United Nations, there is very real opposition in the United States. Anyone who goes to New York is surprised to find the number of publications that are trying to break down the opposition to these specialized agencies and the United Nations in general. While Canada has done something in this connection, our contribution to FAO is just over 2 cents per person per year; to WHO it is under 2 cents; to UNESCO under 2 cents; to ILO under 2 cents, and I think all these organizations are worth more than 2 cents per person per year. If they are, I think the Canadian people must be given more information regarding the problems with which these important organizations are dealing.
I think we should have information regarding the work our Canadian scientists are doing. I have been trying for over a year to find out exactly what sort of work Professor Hardy is doing with FAO in Ceylon. I think it is a pity our Saskatchewan newspapers have not been able to get more information and more particulars regarding his work, which I am sure is outstanding. As a matter of fact, several people who have been out to Ceylon have spoken to me in the very highest terms of the work Professor Hardy has done. I feel it is a great pity it is regarded as such a secret, and that as a result his friends in Saskatchewan cannot get information on the type of work that is done. I think the Minister of National Health and Welfare or external affairs should make available to the Canadian people information concerning the type of work that is being done by Canadians in different parts of the world who are working with WHO.
Before this item carries I hope the secretary of state will make some comments regarding this editorial that has appeared in the two newspapers and my own suggestion, and something to indicate whether or not he might not get more personnel and more money in order to give the Canadian people better information regarding the work of the specialized agencies of the United Nations
Supply-External Affairs that will tie into the needs of the Canadian people, and make them better acquainted with the problems that are being faced, and also to give them more satisfaction as a result of the work their fellow Canadians have been able to do.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to draw the attention of the Prime Minister and the Secretary of State for External Affairs to an article in the July 8 issue of U.S. News and World Report which tells how the United States, during the past year, has come to realize what the communists have known for a long time; that is, that cultural bombardment is an increasingly effective means of winning friends and influencing people abroad.
For a long time the communists have been anxious to show how the nations of this continent, and particularly their great world rival, the United States, are materialistic and culturally barren, and incapable of producing ideals to which the world can cling in difficult times such as these. The communists have been to the forefront for a long time in this movement toward cultural bombardment. But also a number of European nations, even though they were very hard hit by the last world war, have been doing the same thing, though of necessity on a reduced scale.
Until recently the United States and Canada have been the only two western countries of any size and importance that have not subsidized their arts either at home or abroad. Last autumn, however, the United States congress gave the state department a grant of $2,500,000 to help United States artists and athletes make foreign tours which could not hope to meet expenses by commercial bookings. This program was in addition to the libraries, art exhibits and lecturers sponsored by the United States information agency. All these are providing people on every continent with a different view of the North American way of life, which hitherto has been largely portrayed to them through the medium of the movies, which have often given a wrong viewpoint on our way of life on this continent.
Through its art exhibits, their ballet companies, their concert groups, their musical comedies, drama groups and athletic teams, the United States is endeavouring to show peoples in Europe, Asia, Africa and South America that she has a civilization worthy of admiration, one which can express itself with gaiety, good taste and talent.
Canada is known throughout the world mainly for its material assets. We are known principally for our mineral and agricultural wealth, and most people in other countries of the world do not know very much more

Supply-External Affairs about us. We have here in Canada, and we should realize it, cultural assets which we should be proud to show abroad. Just as an example I would mention that during the past few months the National Ballet Company went to Washington, and the reception it received was extremely enthusiastic.. This, I suggest, was of tremendous advantage to Canada. Our Canadian ambassador sent back very enthusiastic reports as to the reception this company received. It was invited on several occasions to attend the Russian embassy and, from the Canadian point of view, the results were very satisfactory.
We have a heritage in this country, and we should be proud to tell the world about it. It stems from both English and French traditions, and has been enriched during the past 50 years by the cultures of people of many other races who have come to settle in our land. I suggest it is up to Canada-and the United States has given us the example- to play our part in the ideological warfare being waged throughout the world today, by showing that a democracy, as we in Canada understand it, can produce cultural and spiritual as well as material assets. We have in Canada artists and artistic groups in most fields of cultural activity which, if given a chance to show themselves abroad, would bring great prestige to Canada and bring us recognition in another, and hitherto unexplored, field.
Thus far-and I hope this will not continue long-the Prime Minister has seemed reluctant to set up the Canada Council, and through this council bring the pleasures of the arts to a greater number of Canadians at home, as well as make it possible to show our arts and artists to people throughout the world. If the Prime Minister would follow the very excellent lead given by the United States congress last fall and make a worth-while grant to the Department of External Affairs, I know well that the Secretary of State for External Affairs would use such a grant wisely. Not only would he make it possible for Canada to play its full part in the ideological warfare, as Russia and other communist countries as well as the United States and other western European countries are doing, but would make it possible to maintain and heighten the artistic standards of the many cultural groups who are striving so hard to maintain themselves in Canada and who, against difficult financial odds, are waging a very successful fight, and a very commendable one indeed.

Mr. Chairman, I have only a few brief comments to make on this first item. I think it must have been noticed by


now that this is one occasion on which there has been almost complete unanimity in the speeches made from both sides of the house. That is perhaps a fortunate thing, as it is always fortunate in a parliament such as ours to have a foreign policy on which we are more or less agreed.
I am particularly happy that on this occasion I have found something in the speech of the Secretary of State for External Affairs as well as that of the Leader of the Opposition with which I am in hearty agreement. In his address this afternoon the Leader of the Opposition coined a phrase which, if not altogether original, certainly is original in this debate, when he said that freedom is not negotiable. I am in hearty accord with him on that point.
I also agreed with him thoroughly when he raised the question of the self-determination of the nations of the world. There can be no doubt at all that in both the Atlantic charter and the charter of the United Nations the principle of self-determination of nations has stood out as the bright hope for the future of all peoples of the world. We know that the attainment of self-determination and full sovereignty is not something which can be accomplished overnight; and people who are in the position of not having full sovereignty are well aware of that fact. But so long as there is a hope, and so long as people who are oppressed feel that the more important nations in the world-and I count Canada in that group-hold firmly to that principle and are prepared to stand up for it and work for it whenever possible, they will be encouraged and will feel that they have friends among us.
The Leader of the Opposition pointed out that there are a number of nations that can be described as satellite states of the Soviet union. It may be said that there are varying degrees in which satellite states may be described. For example there are nations outside the Soviet union but who are so closely related, through military pacts or through straight domination, that they find themselves under the influence of that huge country. Then there are nations which happen to be within the boundaries of the present Soviet union, and which are more directly under its control.
Yet in one respect they are both satellite states. It must always be remembered that not only do we preach and have we preached the self-determination of nations but, as a matter of fact, so has the Soviet union, when it has been found to be a convenient line for them to take. While at times we find that they are apt to deny the freedom of some

of the nations which find themselves within their boundaries in what they describe as a republic state, yet the record shows that whenever it was convenient for them to do so, when they were trying to find allies and friends, particularly in the early part of the revolution when they were not too sure of their own success, the communists themselves were quite glad to promise sovereignty and independence to those nations which now find themselves in a state of bondage within the boundaries of the Soviet union.
For example, on December 17, 1917, Mr. Lenin used the following words in relation to the Ukraine, which today constitutes one of the most important republics within the Soviet union:
We, the soviet of people's commissars, recognize the Ukrainian national republic and its right to separate from Russia or to make an agreement with the Russian republic for federative or other similar mutual relations between them. Everything that touches national rights and the national independence of the Ukrainian people, we, the soviet of people's commissars, accept clearly without limitations and unreservedly.
Nothing could be more categorical than a statement of that kind. It is quite significant to note that it was made on December 17, 1917, at a time when Lenin and his commissars were not too sure as to what would be the final outcome of the revolution. When they felt they needed friends, allies and good neighbours, they at that time offered the hand of friendship and the good neighbour policy to one of the nations beside them. But it is also significant to note, Mr. Chairman, that only eight days later, as a matter of fact on December 25, the same people's commissars issued an ultimatum to the Ukraine in which they practically forced that country to declare itself part of the Soviet union, or else.
Of course we know what happened from there on. The next step was war, and the step after that was the loss of sovereignty by one of the largest nations of Europe. These things have to be remembered and have to be used, because the opportunity does arise from time to time.
We are glad to hear that as a result of the recent talks, meetings and negotiations, perhaps more in the realm of what is unknown than in the realm of what is featured in the headlines, certain things have been accomplished. The general desire for peace in Europe, in the United States, in Great Britain, in Canada, and all over the world is beginning to assert itself. Here I come to the statement with which I so thoroughly agree, made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs. I did not take down the exact words. I would have liked to use them because I liked the sound of them so well, but I think I can
Supply-External Affairs paraphrase them correctly. He said it is well for us to keep a sense of balance at the present time, to go to neither extreme; not to lose sight of the possibility that we may be moving toward peace, nor to lose sight of the fact that we may not be altogether moving away from the realm of danger.
These are wise words in my opinion, Mr. Chairman. If I may be permitted to say so, without intending any offence whatever to our great neighbour to the south, I would say that in my opinion this sense of balance is more evident in our country than it often is amongst our good friends to the south. I think that is one of the reasons Canada is in such a strategic position to be able to play a very important role in the talks that are taking place from time to time, even though we are not considered one of the big four, or even one of the big five.
The influence we can have on international thinking is altogether out of proportion to our population for several reasons. Perhaps the basic reason is the fact that as a nation we have a clean record of international behaviour of which we can feel proud. We can hold up our heads and say that never has Canada coveted the territory of another country. Never have we tried to dominate any nation of the world. We have always stood for what we thought was right. We are four-square behind freedom, and have done everything possible within our resources to play our part in both the old league of nations and in the United Nations at the present time. Therefore Canada stands in a position where she has no skeletons to hide in the closet; we have no shameful episodes to cover up. We are a nation in the international field which, in my opinion, has an excellent record at the present time.
We can very well make up our minds that there are two rather important principles we must always bear in mind. One of these is that we must take a positive attitude at all times. Whenever we do have the opportunity to play our part in international affairs, by positive action, we must know what we are for as a nation as well as what we are against. It is sometimes easy to be against something. Because of the way newspapers normally play up issues, it is not difficult to know what we are opposing, but it is a little more obscure at times to find out just what we are supporting. What are we for? What are the objectives? Our objective must be freedom, freedom not only for ourselves but freedom for other people of the world.
If we are to influence the thinking of the people behind the iron curtain, and not only behind the iron curtain but in satellite states anywhere in the world, then we must make

Supply-External Affairs it perfectly clear that we stand for the selfdetermination of nations, for freedom of all peoples and for a democratic system of government. Then we must also, in following the advice of the Secretary of State for External Affairs, resist the temptation to buy peace at the expense of the peoples who suffer oppression.
I know it is a difficult subject. It is difficult to find the correct point at which we can say we are striving for peace and we shall make certain concessions through negotiation without sacrificing our principles. These are words that are easy to say but in practice, in diplomatic negotiations, they may not be quite as easy to bring about. It is very important that we do not forget there are millions of people in Europe, and perhaps elsewhere, who are looking to countries such as Canada to see what our attitude should be.
Let us never forget either that we must try for the sympathy and friendship of all these people. It is significant that the countries behind the iron curtain and their friends in Canada are not forgetting this. No doubt hon. members received a pamphlet from an outfit which calls itself the "All-Slav Committee of Canada" which announced a conference to be held in Toronto under the name of "The All-Slav Conference". To many members who may not have taken the trouble to look into the details of it, this might have sounded like a sort of cultural get-together of people of Slavic origin.
It may have looked like a harmless sort of affair, but those of us who follow up these things know it is nothing more than another communist front which is trying to play upon the sympathies of people who have some real thoughts and real problems concerning their own nations. They are bold enough, and perhaps sly enough, to come to our country with their propaganda and try to tell us that they are going to get all these people of Slavic origin together in Toronto, that they are going to issue invitations to foreign countries to have them send delegates, they are going to tell the people of Canada what they should do about their own affairs.
This happens to be a free country, and we are proud of it. We are glad to know that we can tolerate that kind of propaganda in our midst. We can even afford perhaps to ignore it and disregard it, which may be the best way of handling it. But let us not forget that if they did not think there was some value in doing that kind of thing they would not be going to the expense and trouble of organizing it. This indicates to us that they feel it is important to play upon the sympathies of people in Canada in relation to their racial origins and so forth, and therefore we should

be prepared to go beyond our boundaries and take advantage of the natural sympathies and friendships which exist among the oppressed people of Europe and perhaps other places.
These are things we have learned as we went along. I hope what the Leader of the Opposition and the Secretary of State for External Affairs have said today will bear fruit, and that when Canada does have an opportunity to play its part, whether it be near the summit or far from the summit, wherever we have influence we will never forget that it is in the interests of this nation to have these millions of allies who are now behind the iron curtain, who in their thinking and in their traditions, who in their culture and their aspirations, are with us in spirit if we will only extend the hand of friendship and show them that we believe firmly in self-determination, freedom and the independence of all nations of the world.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, just before the item carries I think I ought to deal briefly with some of the points that have been raised and some of the questions that were asked during the discussion.
Perhaps I may refer first to the speech of the hon. member for Dauphin. I should like to say how much I agree with what he said and how much I appreciate both the content and spirit of his remarks. How right he was when he said that while we may have to make concessions and compromise in negotiations, we must never sacrifice principles. We will not, I think, in the free democracies accept peace at any price, nor have we any right to ask for peace at no price. The problem is, of course-it is easier stated than solved-what price are we to pay for peace? Another way of putting it is when to stand fast and that of course is the most difficult of all problems in diplomatic negotiations. It is not likely to be any easier in the discussions that are going to take place in the weeks and months ahead.
The hon. member for Broadview made some interesting references to entertainment as a cultural weapon in the propaganda war, or you might wish to put it in a more positive way and refer to it as a cultural link between the nations on either side of the iron curtain as well as between nations who work together politically probably more than they do culturally. I quite agree with the hon. member in his emphasis on the importance of this matter. It is not easy to see where the role of the federal government begins and ends in connection with this subject in a country like Canada, but I do agree with him when he suggests that if the projection of Canada abroad is to be done as impressively

as it should be, an A. Y. Jackson or a ballet dancer or possibly a hockey player can play a part as important as if not a more important part than a visit by the Secretary of State for External Affairs or even possibly by the Minister of National Health and Welfare.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
The Minister of National
Health and Welfare can do the ballet dance, and the Secretary of State for External Affairs can play hockey.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I would like to see the roles reversed. There is, of course, a part to be performed by the government in this field. Anything that can be done properly by the government to show our friends, and those who are not our friends, that we can excel in fields other than the material should be done, but at the same time we have to be careful not to interfere with the responsibilities and rights of the provinces in educational matters and in fields allied to education. That has presented us with a particular difficulty in this country.
Within that limitation we in the federal government have done something, though probably not nearly as much as the hon. member for Broadview and others think we should have done in this field. But as the hon. member indicated, when the Canada Council is set up it will have a special and important part to play in this field. I think any such international activity would be much better done through an agency of that kind than directly by the government. When the Canada Council is set up the role of the government should be, I think, to give that council the necessary support to accomplish what should properly be accomplished in this field. I have no doubt that will be done when action is taken, as indicated by the Prime Minister, to set up this institution.
The hon. member for Greenwood made one interesting and practical suggestion about the importance of the United Nations and how we could recognize this importance by sending to the United Nations assembly ministers of the crown, or indeed as he suggested by having the Prime Minister attend, whenever opportunity offered. I quite agree that the importance of the assembly is minimized when responsible ministers are not able to be there to take part in the discussions. The habit has grown up in recent years of ministers coming for the opening, staying for a week or two and then returning to their capitals. That is understandable as the sessions have increased in length and as the number of items on the agenda has grown. I wish we could do something about it. It is something in the minds, I think, of all the governments of the United Nations, how to
Supply-External Affairs simplify our procedure and reduce the number of items on the agenda. I think that in itself would be an encouragement to ministers to attend more frequently the meetings of the assembly. I do not think the record of Canada in this regard is bad. We have attempted at all times to have at least one and usually have two members of the government represent us as delegates at the United Nations.
The hon. member for Mackenzie made one or two suggestions with which I should like to deal. He has mentioned these to me privately before, and I appreciate his interest. He does not feel that we are doing enough to publicize the activities of the United Nations and its specialized agencies in Canada, with the result that it is difficult to secure information concerning these activities. There again the resources of the federal government are limited. We have not in the Department of External Affairs, nor do I think we should have, a large sum for information activities. I think we have enough to do some of the major jobs in this field, but we are not tempted by a surplus of financial resources to squander unwisely that which we have.
In the field of United Nations publicity we, of course, publish, as the hon. member knows, "Canada and the United Nations". We have an external affairs monthly bulletin in which appear articles on the United Nations and its technical agencies. Then of course there is the United Nations information section itself, whose primary job and main responsibility is to publicize the United Nations in the various countries. The budget of that section of the United Nations secretariat now runs to $4J million, of which Canada contributes $163,000.
Having said that, however, I agree that we might look into this question in order to see whether we could not do more, and do it more effectively. For that purpose, as the hon. member knows, we have set up an interdepartmental committee which has been meeting recently in order to see how more and better information about United Nations activities can be disseminated throughout the country.
The hon. member also mentioned the desirability of exchanges of visits with countries on either side of what we call the iron curtain, and he made special reference to a visit from Canada to Moscow of parliamentarians, and return visits from Moscow. He made some reference also to an invitation which had been sent to me in San Francisco by Mr. Molotov to go to Moscow. So far as parliamentary visits are concerned, there is no possible objection on the part of the

Supply-External Affairs government to a visit by Canadian parliamentarians to the Soviet union. As hon. members know, an invitation or something which has been considered as an invitation has been received. We do not stand on technicalities in this matter. Although the invitation, as hon. members know, is a little unusual, it has been referred to the Speakers of the two houses and I think is something that now should be left in the hands of the Speakers and probably the whips of the various parties.
If it is desired that a visit of that kind should be arranged, certainly no obstacles would be put in its way by the government. On the other hand, a visit from parliamentarians, if I might call them that-although I think I should put inverted commas around that word-from the Soviet union to Canada would, in my opinion, be a matter for the government because the invitation for such a visit might be expected on the other side of the iron curtain to come from the government. I am not sure that this might not be the most useful and interesting way to begin this exchange, namely to have a select group of the Soviet congress-for the moment I cannot recall the exact name of it -come to Canada as guests not of the Soviet embassy or of any particular organization devoted to Canadian-Soviet friendship but as the guests of the government or the parliament-or both-of Canada, to be given an opportunity to see how democracy works in this country.
Such a visit might have a helpful effect on them and it might have a helpful effect on us. Hon. members know that some Soviet agricultural representatives-I am not exactly certain of their political status; I do not think they are members of the Soviet congress, but they might be-are now in the United States, in the state of Idaho, studying agricultural production. That group is coming to Canada on completion of its visit to the United States.
So far as the invitation to myself is concerned, I have already been in touch with the Soviet government through their ambassador here, and arrangements are now being worked out satisfactorily for a visit in October if present plans can be carried through. There is always the possibility of some emergency which may change the arrangements, but if the present plans are carried through I expect to spend a week in the beginning of October in the Soviet union en route to Singapore, where I shall be representing the government at the ministerial meeting of the Colombo plan. It may be that there will be a meeting of the big four foreign ministers in that


month, or there may be some other development which would interfere with such a visit. I would hope that nothing of the sort will happen, and that I shall be able to carry out my plans and accept the invitation for a week's visit to Moscow and the Soviet union while en route to the meeting of the Colombo plan conference at Singapore.
Reference has been made this afternoon, in two statements, I believe, to the Colombo plan, its importance and the desirability of Canada doing everything we can to support this imaginative and important enterprise. This will be an important meeting at Singapore, because at it consideration will be given to the future of the plan, in the light of the extension of its boundaries. More countries have come into the plan in the last year or two. We shall be looking ahead for the next five years-we are approaching the end of the first five years-in order to see what can and should be done to increase and extend the usefulness of what, I think it is generally agreed, has already proved to be an extremely useful development.
I feel greatly privileged at the opportunity of attending this meeting. It will however make it difficult for me to be at the United Nations assembly at that time, Mr. Chairman, and my friend and colleague who is so experienced and skilful in international matters-United Nations matters in particular-* the Minister of National Health and Welfare, will be carrying on there.
I have just one other reference to make, and that is to the interesting and constructive statement made by the Leader of the Opposition this afternoon. In referring to the conferences which are ahead of us-and they will be important ones, possibly even decisive ones-with the other side on security questions, he made a remark which has been repeated by other members in the discussion, namely that freedom is not negotiable. We, of course, all agree with him, Mr. Chairman. Slavery, serfdom, the submergence of peoples by conquest and forced absorption-and that has taken place too often in the last 15 or 20 years-is inconsistent with any kind of peace which is more than enforced submission. Security and slavery, as all history shows, are incompatible. We must therefore all agree, I think, with what he has said on that matter.
But of course that does not solve the problem or answer the question which arises, and he did not attempt to answer the question on this occasion. That question is this. What can we do for those people who, by one method or another, have lost their freedom in the last decade or two but who preserve

in their hearts the national traditions, the cultures, the history and the love of freedom which they were once able to express in political form? As I see it, it does not really help those people who are still, I am quite confident, yearning to be free, if we raise unrealistic hopes of intervention at this time. I refer either to military intervention, which of course would be unrealistic and absurd, or diplomatic intervention which, in certain circumstances, would also be quite unrealistic and which might turn out to do more harm than good to those very people themselves.
I think at the present time the best thing we can do to show that we are still very much aware of their problems and of their situation is to continue to do everything we can to bring about a general pacification, a better state of international affairs, from which they ultimately will be able to benefit. Freedom cannot be killed and it flourishes better, even in submerged peoples, in a generally pacific international climate. It has also a better chance, I think, of expressing itself in political form. Therefore at the present time, while never forgetting the position -and while remembering that there is a relationship between their servitude and our security, we would probably not be well advised to take any step which might react against the people we are trying to help by raising false and premature hopes.
The Leader of the Opposition did suggest that this particular matter was something which might be discussed at the forthcoming meeting of the subcommittee on disarmament, which it was recommended by the big four this afternoon should meet in August of this year. That subcommittee is a technical subcommittee of a larger United Nations committee which has been considering the technical aspects of disarmament now for many months. While I realize it is very difficult indeed to separate the technical and political aspects of this question, I think we have to be very careful about introducing into this particular agency at this particular time political questions which might make it more difficult to close the gap which still exists between the two sides on the technical aspects of the limitation of armaments.
One of the difficulties we have encountered in recent months while the subcommittee was meeting in London was a tendency on the part of the Soviet union, as expressed in its offer of May 10, to try to link up the two things, the political and the technical aspects of disarmament. While not deprecating in any way the importance of this matter I would, therefore, hesitate to agree that the forthcoming subcommittee meeting in New York on disarmament would be the best place
Supply-External Affairs to thresh out this question. Possibly a meeting of foreign ministers on the political level would be more appropriate for that purpose; but even there, as the Geneva meetings which have just concluded show, it is a subject which has to be handled, as it was handled by President Eisenhower, with care as well as with frankness.
I think I have at least touched on the points that have been raised this afternoon, but before I sit down I should like to express my appreciation, and I am sure it is an appreciation which is shared by all of us, that this discussion has shown, as have other discussions on external affairs, that there is an underlying and encouraging unity in this house on the broad questions of principle in this field.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I do not intend to take more than a few minutes to deal with one aspect of the remarks of the Secretary of State for External Affairs. I do not wish to leave any possible impression on the record, and I am not suggesting that there was any thought of doing so except by the reference to the subject, that I was proposing that there should be intervention, either direct or indirect, as a means of solving the extremely important question of the freedom of those nations which have been enslaved since the war. I have made it clear on other occasions that I believe this must be made a part of general discussions, and that there are many occasions when this can be presented to Russia along with the proposals that the Soviets make to Canada and other countries.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs has said, what can we do for those people who have lost their freedom? He went on to say that it does not help to raise false hopes. I agree with that. Nevertheless, subjects have been discussed which appear unlikely to be solved at an early date. Russia, for instance, did not hesitate for a moment to raise certain questions in connection with German unification. Nor, on the other hand, did we hesitate to raise questions about German unification knowing that Russia held different views.
I think there should be a constant reiteration to the Russians of the demand that they remember their obligations. I raised the question at a time when the Secretary of State for External Affairs was not here because he was attending the celebration in San Francisco of the tenth anniversary of the signing of the charter of the United Nations. I dealt then with the points made by Mr. Molotov at San Francisco, when he raised certain questions about the entry of communist China into the United Nations and other subjects that are highly controversial.
6692	HOUSE OF
Supply-External Affairs He did not hesitate to raise these questions there. Surely if Russia can raise the prospect of the entry of communist China into the United Nations we have an equal right, without raising false hopes, to say on similar occasions and at similar meetings that while the Russians are saying to us there are certain things that should be done, we say to them that here is something fundamental to be done.
At San Francisco Mr. Molotov went so far as to say that there should be evidence of deeds and not words. He went so far as to tell the western nations that they should give positive evidence of their desire for peace. I think if Mr. Molotov or any other representative of the Russian government is to make suggestions of that kind at San Francisco or elsewhere, it is appropriate for us to say to them that the very best positive evidence that can be offered of a desire for peace is to comply with their own undertakings at San Francisco on an earlier occasion, when they gave the absolutely unqualified assurance that they would give a free vote to the nations then occupied by their armies. In fact they even went so far as to say how it was to be done. They were going to bring in representatives of the democratic elements in those countries and add them to the provisional governments already set up, so the base could be laid for a free vote under a government of that kind.
I am simply pointing out that the Russians have not hesitated to make suggestions as to things they think should be done. I do not see any reason why we should hesitate-and when I say "we" I mean Canada-because I think as far as the central purpose is concerned there is complete unanimity on the part of all of us. I do not think there is any reason why we should hesitate to say to Russia that here is a very fundamental thing you could do to demonstrate your belief by deeds and not words in the cause of peace.
I think just as long as there are scores of millions of people living in slavery, contrary to the unqualified undertaking of the Russian government, denied the right to have a vote which would offer them the self-determination that was set forth in the beginning of the United Nations charter, we actually are leaving the possibility of explosive forces being created which at any time could cause difficulties for all of us no matter what agreements may be made.
I think recently we have seen evidence even in this house of the value of reiteration, and in the larger field I think that reiteration may finally impress itself. Without any expectation that there may be intervention of any kind, and I wish to make that quite


clear, I would hope that we would reiterate our demand. As the Russians put forward their ideas, we also should put forward our belief that just as certain areas and countries were given a vote after the first world war under the league of nations, a similar vote could be provided under the United Nations by which people would be able to have the right to determine their own form of government, a right assured at San Francisco and at the meetings which preceded the San Francisco conference. I repeat that there is no difference on either side of the house with regard to the central purpose we are all seeking to serve.
We all want to see what can be done to bring about the reality of peace. The remarks I made were directed certainly not to the raising of false hopes but merely to the assurance that could be extended to our friends, who deep in their hearts believe in the same things as we do, that we have not forgotten them and will continue to seek to impress upon the Russian government that it live up to its written obligation given some years ago when the charter of the United Nations was signed.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
In agreeing with what the Leader of the Opposition has just said, I think I should add that I and the other Canadian delegates at the United Nations and at other places have, both in public and in private, stated and restated to the delegates of communist countries our understanding of the importance of this obstacle to peace and security, the obstacle being the lack of freedom of those countries which were promised freedom years ago.
We shall be glad to do that again as the opportunity offers, and the opportunity is offering itself now in connection with Germany because there is a part of Germany which is not free within our meaning of the word. The western powers have taken their stand very firmly, and they reiterated that stand at Geneva, and we associate ourselves in Canada with it, that there can be no reunification of Germany except on the basis of free elections; there can be no security in Europe until Germany is reunited on that basis.

While I have no intention of bringing up numerous matters, there are two or three I want to mention, and there is one that apparently should come under this item. The details appear at page 173, and it is a vote of $344,000 for telephones, telegrams and other communications. It is about double what it was the year before, and that is what moves me to ask for an explanation of it.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: This matter came up in the committee, Mr. Chairman, and it was dealt with in some detail at page 643 of the committee report for June 2. I do not want to go into the details, but I would merely say to my hon. friend that the increase is largely due to bringing up to date and modernizing our whole communications and cipher equipment, which is a very expensive business but which has become increasingly necessary as our communications have grown and have become more important in the offices we have all over the world.
Will a good deal be capital and non-recurring?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes, a great deal is capital.

This is not really a question, but rather a matter of clarification. I am doing this, I hope, as a favour to the minister. In his reply he made one statement which, unfortunately, could lend itself to a very bad interpretation if it were taken literally. In dealing with these submerged nations he made this statement, as I took it down: "There is a relationship between their servitude and our security." I hope I know what he meant, but certainly it could be interpreted to mean that the latter is only attainable at the expense of the former, and I should like to give him an opportunity to clarify the statement to make sure the meaning is clear.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I am grateful to the hon. member, because what I had in mind was exactly the opposite of the interpretation which the hon. member says, and quite rightly, might be given to those remarks. What I had in mind to say was that as long as they are in servitude the rest of the world cannot feel secure.

I hesitate to bring this
matter up, yet I think we must face it. What caused world war II? What caused the war with Germany? It was the fact that Germany needed markets and she needed raw materials. Let us just face that fact without any nonsensical remarks. Germany urgently needed markets and raw materials. It is not going to be very long before this industrialization now beginning to prevail in Germany will render her need for markets imperative and her need for raw materials equally imperative.
Now, what brought about the war between Japan and this country? It was exactly the same thing. Japan wanted markets and she wanted raw materials. She wanted to exploit China as a source of markets and raw materials.
Supply-External Affairs
What I would like to ask the minister is this. Does anyone at any of these conferences he attends ever give any attention to that kind of thing? I am not particularly concerned about whether or not the minister answers tonight. But for us to go forward as though this problem did not exist is for us to betray our trust. Someone said this afternoon, I believe it was the Leader of the Opposition, that we must give attention to history; we must give attention to what has already occurred.
One of the greatest weaknesses of the whole United Nations set-up, when it was planned at Dumbarton Oaks and established at San Francisco, was that inadequate attention was given to this very important matter of markets for all. The people at those conferences acted as though the problem did not exist.
What I am wondering about is, are we going to be wise enough to make allowance for these needs; because remember if Germany's need for raw materials and markets becomes imperative, all the United Nations on earth will not stop her. The same thing will be true of Japan. And even if we could stop these peoples, we would but force them into economic servitude.
We do not have to go outside this wonderful country of ours, this Canada, to get an illustration. Let us take the situation of the maritimes. What is the difficulty in respect of the maritimes? They cannot develop industry. And why? There is a reason. They cannot have their own markets. And why is that? The main reason is that Ontario and Quebec want to develop the industry. They want to get all the markets.
Now, if you just apply that same situation to the world, you have all the explosiveness necessary to set the world on fire in a war. I hope that some time before long we will begin to talk as though we realized that fundamentally nations fight for markets and for raw materials. Until we organize this world in such a way that we can provide all the people who wish to produce with markets, and all the peoples who wish to produce with a suitable source of raw materials, then it is utterly idle to talk about having a free, peaceful, prosperous or happy world.
If the minister feels like replying now, without having time to prepare, well and good. If he does not, he may just leave this little contribution to be thought about in the future.

speechtext: Payments under the Colombo plan cover both capital assistance and technical assistance.
