Can the minister say anything as to the likely duration of our participation?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I can say that it is a matter which has been giving us a great deal of thought and some worry in the department, because at the present time there are about 170 Canadians serving on the international commissions in the three Indo-Chinese states. We think it will go on for another year. We had rather hoped, when the commissions were formed, that they would be able to accomplish their purposes in two years. The first stage of the work has been pretty successfully accomplished in regrouping the forces behind the 17th parallel in Viet Nam, and the restoration of order and some form of security in the other states. I cannot predict with certainty, but we hope that within another year at the most our obligations in regard to these commissions will be discharged.
Are recent disorders a serious threat to the accomplishment of the commission?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Well, the recent riots at Saigon have been a deplorable development; and the commission, which has just moved from Hanoi, where it was in northern Viet

Nam, to Saigon-or is about to move to Saigon-has naturally viewed with some anxiety the prospect of carrying on its activities in Saigon in view of these riots. However, it is to be hoped that sufficient security precautions will be taken by the authorities in question to prevent a recurrence of this sort of thing in the future.
The commissions are in touch with the governments concerned, the government of Viet Nam and the government of France, which has a residual responsibility for security there, and as a result of these contacts in the last day or two we hope the commission will be able to carry on its work satisfactorily in Viet Nam.

When the minister gives the figure of the number of Canadians involved it makes me realize that I have had a wrong idea of the nature of the work of the commission. I had thought of it as something in the nature of a judicial or reviewing body. But when the minister refers to 170 persons, I realize it must be doing much more than that.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The 170 persons consist largely of officers of the Canadian armed services, or mobile and stationary inspection teams, to see that the military clauses of the armistice are carried out. Of that 170 there are only about 35 civilians from the Department of External Affairs in the three Indo-Chinese countries.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE Civil defence-
283. To provide for the civil defence program, $7,001,034.

Mr. Chairman, by a very strange coincidence it was 9.35 p.m. last Saturday night we entered upon the discussion of this item, and I notice that tonight, a week later, it is 9.31 p.m. So may I point out that once again we are in the very awkward position, toward the end of a long session, of being compelled to discuss civil defence in just a few minutes. I think it reflects a very bad arrangement of the business of the house when civil defence is relegated to such an inferior position in relation to other matters coming before us.
May I point out that this is nothing new. I looked back to see what had happened in 1952. On the subject of civil defence we spent one hour and 20 minutes. I estimate the time by allowing seven minutes per page of Hansard. In 1953 we spent 50 minutes on the subject of civil defence. In 1954 a little more attention was paid to it, two
Supply-Health and Welfare hours and a half. This year, 1955, so far we have had 25 minutes on this subject.
A week ago I was prepared for two things. Had the minister risen in his place and made a statement on civil defence I would have been prepared to continue past the hour of ten o'clock, but he was asked to make a statement and failed to do so. That has been his practice for the past four years. I think it is wrong. I think the minister should lead off, summarize the work and give us an indication of what is going on rather than sit it out, as he did last year, have half a dozen people speak and then rise and comment on each suggestion that was made.
We are not in a position, really, to make suggestions unless we know the picture of civil defence. I purposely restrict my remarks this evening in order to give the minister a chance to tell us just what is going on in civil defence. I could easily consume the allotted time on the subject, since I have been looking into it, but I am not going to do so, in the hope that the minister will tell us just what is happening in his department. He must give us some assistance, because we are not in a very happy position on civil defence. In my opinion there is too much misunderstanding. The minister is coming in for a great deal of criticism with regard to lack of plans, and so on.
I hold in my hand four articles from the Winnipeg Free Press of March of this year, which talk about plans which do not exist. I am not going to quote from them. I have articles from the Winnipeg Tribune, dated March 1, reporting a speech made by the chief instructor of Canada's civil defence college. The speech was made at Arnprior. The heading says "Grim Forecast for Montreal and Toronto. A Million Dead without Warning." Then I have other information concerning the results of the recent tests at Nevada which have a bearing on civil defence.
My hope was that the minister would have brought us up to date on this matter. I am not going to suggest that things are not going well in civil defence. I am not going to enter into that discussion or make a detailed analysis of what is going on. Take it for granted that co-operation is essential between the provinces and the federal government and between the municipalities and the provincial governments, and so on. I take all that for granted. What we need to know now is the actual situation, because the general impression appears to be that in the event of the explosion of a hydrogen bomb, everybody is going to be destroyed. We have read quite a bit in the newspapers about the danger of fall-out, yet at the same time we find that
6696	HOUSE OF
Supply-Health and Welfare in the Nevada tests people in trenches quite close to that particular explosion survived. Several lessons were learned from that test. We had Canadian observers there.
The minister should select the House of Commons as the place to make statements concerning these things. I do not like to be dependent upon newspaper accounts, because everybody knows that if we suggest to the minister that he was reported as having made a speech in such and such a place regarding civil defence he might, quite properly and rightly, say that was not the full account of what he said. Perhaps this speech at Arnprior was not correctly reported. It is only in a statement made here in the house, recorded in Hansard, that we can have accurate information with regard to this subject.
I hope the minister will be able to tell us that there is a chance for survival without complete evacuation of cities; or if we are dependent on evacuating cities then how are the plans going with regard to that? I find it rather confusing, yet how important the whole problem is.
We are building very expensive radar warning lines in the north in order to give us warning of impending attack. We are counting on interceptor planes to prevent bombers reaching us. We are living in some trepidation of the development of intercontinental rockets which might strike without warning. So I should say, despite the talks that are now going on at Geneva, we cannot immediately forget all our defensive plans, and part of those is civil defence.
A year ago the minister said-and I again appreciate what he said-we do not need to build the thing up, get excited about it and go in for quite a bit of ballyhoo. I quite agree. Civil defence should be considered very coldly and dispassionately, and not made a matter of tremendous excitement. The Canadian people are sensible enough to deal with these matters provided that they know what to do.
Well, now, Mr. Chairman, I could go on at very considerable length. I would have liked to do so, to have analysed some of the forecasts and given some regard to suggestions that were made last year, to have commented upon the minister's statement of last year, but I am going to conclude in just one minute and give others a chance to participate.
Specifically I would ask the minister to tell us now of the danger from the hydrogen bomb from the standpoint of the experts who have studied these matters. Let him also tell us whether or not our sole means of safety is in the evacuation of cities, or whether at the same time bomb-proof shelters might be desirable. In that connection, I am sure he


has seen the experiment being undertaken by the Toronto Telegram in erecting a bombproof shelter which they say was inspired by the minister and has been approved by General Worthington.
These are the things that confuse the public. Is everybody to rush out of the cities after warning, or are they to provide protection for themselves, or is there to be public protection? What is the plan at the present time? Let us not just throw up our hands in horror and say nothing can be done. I feel sure a great many things can be done in this struggle for survival, and we should not simply be discouraged because of the scare headlines that we have read. Therefore it is a matter of responsibility for the minister to relieve the minds of Canadian people and point us in the right direction.

Mr. Chairman, I must say I, and I am sure the house generally, sympathize with what the hon. gentleman said at the outset. Hon. members will recall that last week, after the hon. member for Notre Dame de Grace spoke, I offered-it is true it was after ten o'clock-to intervene. The reason I did so was that I thought that was the most orderly way of proceeding at that time.
I fully agree with the hon. member that this subject, like so many other subjects we have to discuss at this time, justifies full consideration. I am sure he will appreciate, just as other hon. members will appreciate, that none of us individually is the author of this particular situation. I thank my hon. friend for what I thought were fair remarks on his part. As the Leader of the Opposition acknowledged in this house, this is perhaps the most difficult matter facing modern governments at this time. Certainly I would not for one moment suggest that in this country or in any other country of the free world we have reached anything like the stage where we can speak of this matter with satisfaction in so far as our actual preparations are concerned.
As the former prime minister of Great Britain, Sir Winston Churchill, said three months ago, that is the situation. It is true, as the President of the United States said a short time ago. It is true, as I have said repeatedly. My hon. friend has said that he is not now speaking of the conventional side of civil defence, that he appreciates there is a great measure of co-operation in this matter, much greater now than there was in an earlier period. We can confirm that. For instance, we now have an agreement with the senior province, that is the largest province, as to the sharing of costs and as to the division of responsibility. I cannot speak

too highly of the co-operation we are receiving at this time from the province of Ontario, as we are receiving co-operation from practically all the other provinces.
That co-operation is necessary because, as I have stated repeatedly, civil defence depends in the final analysis upon the action of the individual citizen. If Coventry does not want to be defended, no government in the United Kingdom can defend the people of Coventry. Those were the words of Mr. Churchill, and one could paraphrase those words and apply them to Canada. I think we can say that on the conventional side of civil defence we are as advanced as, in some particulars even more advanced than, other countries.
We have now registered 189,000 civil defence workers as compared with 300,000 civil defence workers registered in the United Kingdom. On a per capita basis we have more civil defence workers than they have in the country to the south. On a per capita basis our grants to the municipalities are greater than those in the United States. In both the United Kingdom and Canada the central government does not bear the full cost. In our case we bear roughly 90 per cent of the cost. In the United Kingdom the grants to the municipalities are slightly greater than are our grants to the provinces, and our grants to the provinces and to the municipalities are larger than those in the United States.
My hon. friend says he assumes that the things we have been saying about the conventional side of civil defence should be accepted. He has touched upon the most difficult problem we have to face, that is the implications of	the thermonuclear
weapon. We have to realize and we do realize that the primary information comes to us from the United States. That is the only country on our side which has the necessary bombs, and it is the only country which has carried on tests in connection with them. We have had the opportunity of having our officials witness these tests, both on the military and civil defence sides. We are collaborating continually with the United Kingdom and United States civil defence officials, and the plans and operations we have under way likewise parallel the plans and operations in the United States and the United Kingdom.
Last week we had a conference here on civil defence at which Governor Val Peterson, director of civil defence in the United States, and his associates were present. We exchanged views, as did General Worthington at the meeting of NATO civil defence units in Paris where he had the opportunity 50433-423
Supply-Health and Welfare of conferring with his opposite numbers in the United Kingdom, the Scandinavian countries and the United States.
My hon. friend touched on a difficult problem when he said the Canadian people do not want to be panicked, they do not want to be frightened. We are criticized at one point because we do not say enough; we are criticized on the other hand because on occasion we do frighten our people. My hon. friend was probably referring to a speech I made a short time ago at the civil defence college. What I said then was true. I quite realize that in saying that if a thermonuclear bomb were dropped on the city of Toronto at a certain level with certain winds prevailing west to east it would cause the death of a million people. That is a frightening statement, but that was not the first time that statement had been made. I have been criticized for not making enough statements of that kind. My hon. friend will appreciate the difficulty of knowing precisely where to draw the line.
The best knowledge available-I do not speak only of Canada but of other countries as well-is that assuming the worst, assuming the dropping of a thermonuclear bomb on a community, the people within a certain radius of that direct primary target area would be completely annihilated.
Whether above or below ground?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Yes. My hon. friend has had a chance of verifying the observations made recently by British scientists who made representations particularly to the Prime Minister of Great Britain. What they said was true. I am not saying that this will eventuate, because it may be that the Prime Minister of Britain was right when he said that the very cataclysmic potential of the bomb would be such as to make it in terms of desirable human conduct impossible to happen, but we cannot make that assumption. The fact is that the best knowledge available now suggests-there are implications in this for the military that we have to bear in mind, and I am sure my hon. friend will understand-that the best defence against that kind of attack is evacuation.
The evacuation of Canadian communities has been studied and acted upon. This is the only known defence against that particular weapon. With that in view, and impossible as the task may seem, we in civil defence in this country and elsewhere have evolved plans for evacuation. I do not say that at this moment we could evacuate all the communities of Canada, because we could not and
6698	HOUSE OF
Supply-Health and Welfare neither could the United States, the United Kingdom or other countries. But it does not help us to have some people say that evacuation is an impossibility. It may be impossible in certain areas-I will not say what areas- but surely it is not impossible in a country like Canada, with our open spaces and our relatively small number of large communities. In certain sections of the United States the problem becomes one of the greatest magnitude.
We have carried on evacuations in this country. We had an evacuation last fall in Brockville. We had an evacuation in May in St. John's, Newfoundland. We had a successful evacuation about six weeks ago in Brandon, Manitoba. In the month of September we are going to have the largest and the most complete form of evacuation ever attempted on the continent with the exception of that carried out in one United States city.
When we talk about this problem it is not merely a question of moving people out of a building or moving people out of a city. The question involves many auxiliary services such as hospitalization, welfare, billeting and so on. Admittedly it becomes one of the most difficult tasks that has ever been attempted, but one is driven to do something about this matter because there is no other defence known to us at this time. I merely mention these details to indicate to the hon. gentleman that this matter is very much in our minds, as it is in the minds of those in other countries similarly engaged.
With regard to the fall-out, may I say that is one of the further implications of this problem. A bomb falling on the particular city mentioned, with the wind prevailing west to east, would cause havoc as far away as the city of Sherbrooke in the province of Quebec through the dangers of the fall-out. The known ways of dealing with the fall-out have been tested in the Nevada desert, and we are taking advantage of that experience. It is not our own experience. It is the experience of those who have the bomb and who have tried it out. On the basis of what they have tested I have made, in general terms, these observations. We do know that there are certain forms of shelter against the fall-out. There is the ordinary basement, the shelter underground with three feet of earth on top and so on. These have all been tested. They are being tested in Canada as they have been tested in Nevada.
As to the particular story that appeared in the Toronto Telegram, I can only say that I have not seen that shelter. However, I did say that this kind of interest was to be


commended and that we were looking at the particular shelter in order to see whether or not it conforms to what, in the light of the Nevada experience, seems to be an effective kind of shelter. I have not yet had a report on the matter.
I hope I have given my hon. friend an indication that we appreciate the problem we face. I have given him a general outline of the kind of work we are seeking to do. I would invite him and other hon. members, at their leisure, to go to the civil defence college at Arnprior. We have now trained there, completely at federal expense, almost 7,000 individuals, who in turn have trained 83,000 individuals who are engaged in various activities throughout the country.
I do not want to detain the house needlessly at this time. I am answering directly the observations made by my hon. friend. I have made these observations to show him our interest in the matter. I am prepared to answer any other questions. I want the house to know that with all the power and energy we possess-in collaboration with the other countries, with the provinces and with 800 different communities in Canada-we are seeking to focus our attention at our organization levels on what I am sure all hon. members will recognize as the most difficult task one could possibly assume.
It is sometimes suggested that this is a problem for the Department of National Defence. At one time this matter was under that department. I remember the observations made by the hon. member for Cape Breton South last year and also by the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich, who agreed that this was essentially a civil responsibility. That is the experience in the United Kingdom, and it is the experience in the United States.
There is a role for the armed forces to play. My colleague the Minister of National Defence and I have had consultations with one another about further studies to be made on the part to be played by the military in this country. There is a role, I would hope, for the reserve to play in certain phases of civil defence. But we must not forget that civil defence is essentially the welfare services, the police services, the fire services, the medical services and the health services of the community. There is a role for others to play in this activity, which at this time is essentially a civilian activity.
My hon. friend may be sure that I greatly appreciate the remarks he made and the tenor of his approach.

There is one aspect of civil defence which I have not heard mentioned,

though I assume that it must have had consideration. I should just like to ask a question if I can do so within the time that is left. Let us assume that there has been a destructive thermonuclear battle which has -as well it might-destroyed the capital of Canada and the provincial capitals, and you have all the problems the minister has been discussing with regard to saving people. What I am concerned about is the survival of the national entity, particularly the federal civil administrative authority. If the minister could, in a few words, say whether that matter has received any thought, I should be glad if he would do so.
I should like him to tell us how the powers which are exercised by this house and our government devolve if the country has been broken up into pockets of resistance. There must be in existence some plan by which those in a local community can recognize who represents the civil authority in that area, assuming that the centres have been destroyed. Perhaps I have not expressed my thought fully but I do not want to take the necessary time to do so. That is, however, the sort of problem I have in mind, namely the devolution of civil authority throughout the country. People should know where to look if that incredible situation should develop; and that is the problem I have in mind.

That problem is very much to the fore. It is a matter that was discussed at the last NATO meeting about three weeks ago. NATO has made certain recommendations to the member states of the North Atlantic community. We are now giving consideration to them. It is also one of the matters that we discussed with the United States a few days ago.
I think the minister has not quite followed me, or I have not fully expressed my thought. I am looking toward the continuing civil authority, not the military authority.

Yes, I know. The NATO meeting I referred to is the civil defence meeting under NATO auspices. Under NATO the civil defence forces of the NATO countries meet. They are not the military; they are the civil defence authorities. General Worthington represented us at the last one, with General Sir Sidney Kirkman of the United Kingdom and Governor Peterson of the United States.
Carried.

Mr. Chairman, if we leave this matter where it stands now I think it is not fair to this committee or to the minister. I am going to read one sentence from a speech 50433-423J
Supply-Health and Welfare I myself made a year ago. It is just one sentence and not a very long one. As reported at page 6498 of Hansard of June 22, 1954, it is as follows:
If we had a bombing attack tomorrow the minister would be grievously and very unfairly blamed for what would be the fault of us all, and I suggest therefore that we be given a very realistic appreciation of this situation as it is and not as we would like it to be.
I feel that what the minister has done tonight has been to give us some illustrations of what is going on. He has mentioned evacuations from small places where the problem is a tiny one compared with what it would be with respect to Montreal or Toronto. I like to think I am speaking in the minister's interest as well as in the interest of this house.
I suggest that we have not the information which this house should have. The task which he has is unbelievably difficult, because it is almost beyond human capacity to stir people up to do what they should do themselves. I am not going to make a speech tonight, but I suggest again that at the present moment, in spite of what the minister says about the people they have trained and in spite of the other things he has mentioned, as a matter of fact he has not made an impact on the people of Canada to this moment. It is his job to do so, however hard-and perhaps unfairly hard-it is. Therefore I hope that the minister will make a full statement. If he wants to know what I mean by a full statement, I suggest that he look at the speech made a year ago by the hon. member for Calgary North. It was set out there in considerable detail. I submit again, Mr. Chairman, that we are not doing our duty if we pass this item at this moment.
Carried.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Shall the item carry?

I was wondering if the
minister would clear up one thing. The point that was disturbing me was the results of the Nevada test, as reported in the newspapers. I do not know how accurate these reports are. I have no information as to the size of the bomb that was exploded in that test. The minister may be talking about something a great deal larger. However, in an editorial in the Montreal Gazette of the 7th of May there is the following:
Survival is possible within a fairly close range of an atomic blast, if suitable shelter is available . . . The lesson is that survival Is possible for many of the people in a target area. . . . First, there must be adequate shelter, public or private. This could be anything from a masonry office building to a good cellar, or a trench in a back yard. Second, there must be trained teams of

Supply-Health and Welfare
radiation experts in the area to assess damage, discover and patrol danger areas and supply first aid and reorganization.
Do the plans of the minister cover both aspects, that is protection of that nature within the target area plus plans for evacuation? That is the point that I think is not quite clear.

Yes, they do. The bomb in the Nevada test to which my hon. friend has referred was one equivalent to 36,000 tons of TNT. That is about twice the size of the bomb dropped at Nagasaki. The bomb dropped at the Eniwetok atoll in November, 1953, was of course a thermonuclear bomb, and the United States government has not decided to drop a bomb of that dimension on the mainland. We rely for our estimate of the danger of the thermonuclear bomb, the kind dropped on the Eniwetok atoll, on the experience that was obtained from that particular detonation. But we are able to make certain conclusions by comparing the damage caused by the 36 kiloton bomb dropped at Nevada with the damage caused on the islands in the Eniwetok atoll. Our conclusions are also based on other considerations, but I am sure my hon. friend will understand that I cannot give them in public.

Would it not be better to attempt to get the idea across that survival is possible even in the case of a hydrogen or atomic bomb attack? What I fear is that the present apathy is due to the fact many people think nothing can be done, and I suggest that the emphasis should be placed on the fact that it is possible to survive if precautions are taken.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Perhaps my hon. friend has seen the material that has been issued recently and the notes on other material that are coming out along that very line, pointing out what can be done. We are now sending out specifications as to the kind of shelters which could be used under certain circumstances. My hon. friend made what I thought was a very helpful observation tonight. I am not comparing it with what the hon. member for Greenwood had to say, but the hon. member for Greenwood did take another position which reflects the situation in which we find ourselves. We could go all out and do what they are doing in another country. I have been in hotels in another country and I have seen signs and all that sort of thing.
I have talked to the civil defence directors in 36 United States cities, and I am satisfied that in what we are doing here we are building on as solid lines as we possibly can, and


we are doing it in what I believe the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre referred to as the Canadian manner. It may not satisfy everyone.
On this very point I recently met a group of individuals representing various organizations who have special experience in the dissemination of information. One representative was the hon. member for Notre Dame de Grace representing the Canadian federation of advertising and sales clubs. We had a conference with this group, and we are now taking into consideration some of their recommendations. Some of them are pretty much along the lines of those we have been following.

Last year when some of us visited the civil defence college at Arnprior we were shown a little gadget which looked something like a pencil flashlight. As I recall, its purpose was to enable an individual to determine whether or not he was radioactive, and it was suggested then that there was going to be a program of distribution. Can the minister tell us what has been done in that connection?

The hon. member is referring to the dosimeters shown to the people who visited the civil defence college. We had hoped that in February we would be able to approve for general distribution that particular model. However, in the light of the experience with regard to that dosimeter at Nevada we have decided to withhold approval for the time being. A new one is now under consideration. I hope we will be able to make some assessment as to its use by September, and if it meets our requirements I hope we can recommend it for the kind of distribution we had intended.
